title: Time and Space Efficiency
text:
Efficiency is about solving problems with a sensible amount of time and memory. In data science, performance matters because datasets can be large and analysis pipelines can be repeated many times.
A clear understanding of efficiency helps you choose the right approach before the code becomes too slow or too expensive in memory to use.

title: Time and Space Efficiency
text:
Algorithmic complexity
Big O notation describes how an algorithm’s running time grows as the size of the input increases. It captures the dominant cost for large inputs.
Common complexity classes:

O(1) — constant time: the cost does not change when input size grows.
O(n) — linear time: the cost grows in proportion to the number of items.
O(n log n) — linearithmic time: common for efficient sorting.
O(n^2) — quadratic time: often caused by nested loops.
O(2^n) — exponential time: grows extremely fast with input size.







NoteIn a nutshell: what these classes feel like



The labels make more sense with a tangible task on n items:







Class
A tangible example




O(1)
Asking one student their name.


O(n)
Reading every student’s name once down the register.


O(n log n)
Sorting the register into alphabetical order.


O(n^2)
Comparing every student against every other student (every pair).


O(2^n)
Listing every possible group (subset) the students could form.



The further down the table, the faster the cost explodes as the class grows.

title: Time and Space Efficiency
text:
Space efficiency
Space efficiency describes how much memory an algorithm or operation needs as the input grows.
Common space categories:

O(1) — constant space: uses a fixed amount of memory regardless of input size.
O(n) — linear space: memory grows in proportion to the input.
O(n^2) — quadratic space: memory grows with the square of the input size.

Many data analysis operations are linear in space because they create vectors or tables that are proportional to the dataset.

title: Time and Space Efficiency
section: Example: time and space in R
text:
Example: time and space in R

Loop vs vectorised squaring
A direct loop computes squared values one element at a time:


Code
```{r}
n <- 1000000
x <- rnorm(n)
y <- numeric(n)
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  y[i] <- x[i] ^ 2
}
```


This has:

time complexity roughly O(n),
space complexity O(n) because the result vector y grows with the input size.

The vectorised version does the same work more compactly:


Code
```{r}
y <- x ^ 2
```


It still uses O(n) time and O(n) space, but the work is performed inside a compiled routine and avoids the overhead of the explicit R loop.


Time vs memory trade-off
If you only need the squared values and not the original vector, you can overwrite x:


Code
```{r}
x <- x ^ 2
```


This still uses O(n) time, but it avoids keeping both x and y in memory at the same time. If you need both, then memory usage is higher.

title: Time and Space Efficiency
Time and Space Efficiency
text:
Recursion and the call stack
So far our examples have used iteration (loops) to repeat work. A second way to repeat work is recursion, where a function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs two parts:

a base case that stops the recursion, and
a recursive case that moves the problem closer to the base case.

A classic example is the factorial \(n! = n \times (n-1) \times \dots \times 1\):


Code
```{r}
factRec <- function(n) {
  if (n <= 1) {
    return(1)          # base case
  }
  n * factRec(n - 1)  # recursive case
}

factRec(5)
```


[1] 120



The hidden space cost
Recursion has a space cost that loops do not. Each time a function calls itself, R must remember where it was so it can resume once the inner call returns. It does this by adding a stack frame to the call stack. The frames are only cleared once the base case is reached and the calls unwind.
This means a recursion that goes n levels deep uses O(n) space on the call stack, even if it returns a single number. The equivalent loop uses O(1) space:


Code
```{r}
factIter <- function(n) {
  res <- 1
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    res <- res * i
  }
  res
}

factIter(5)
```


[1] 120


Both are O(n) in time, but the loop keeps memory flat while the recursion grows the stack.






Warning



R does not optimise tail-recursion, and it caps recursion depth (see options(expressions = ...)). Very deep recursion will throw a “evaluation nested too deeply” / stack overflow error. For deep problems in R, prefer iteration or vectorisation.




When recursion is expensive in time, too
Recursion can also hide a severe time cost if the same sub-problems are recomputed. The naive Fibonacci sequence makes two recursive calls each step, so the work doubles at every level — O(2^n) time, the worst class from our table above:


Code
```{r}
fibRec <- function(n) {
  if (n < 2) return(n)        # base cases: fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1
  fibRec(n - 1) + fibRec(n - 2)
}

system.time(fibRec(27))
```


   user  system elapsed 
   0.14    0.00    0.15 


The same sequence computed iteratively is O(n) time and O(1) space — astronomically faster:


Code
```{r}
fibIter <- function(n) {
  a <- 0; b <- 1
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    new <- a + b
    a <- b
    b <- new
  }
  a
}

system.time(fibIter(27))
```


   user  system elapsed 
      0       0       0 








Note



Recursion is not “bad” — it often expresses an algorithm far more clearly than a loop (the Euclidean algorithm and Newton-Raphson method in the Mathematics to Code section are natural recursions). The lesson is to be aware of its two costs: stack space proportional to depth, and repeated time if sub-problems overlap. When overlap happens, memoisation (caching results) or an iterative rewrite restores efficiency.








TipGoing further 🚀



Memoisation caches each result the first time it is computed, so every sub-problem is solved once — collapsing fibRec’s O(2^n) time down to O(n) without rewriting the recursion. The memoise package wraps any function for you:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(memoise)
fibMemo <- memoise(fibRec)   # cache lives in the wrapper
system.time(fibMemo(40))     # near-instant; naive fibRec(40) would hang
```


Under the hood it is just a lookup table. You can build a tiny one by hand with a base-R environment as the cache:


Code
```{r}
cache <- new.env()
fibCached <- function(n) {
  key <- as.character(n)
  if (!is.null(cache[[key]])) return(cache[[key]])   # already known?
  val <- if (n < 2) n else fibCached(n - 1) + fibCached(n - 2)
  cache[[key]] <- val                                # store for next time
  val
}
fibCached(40)
```


[1] 102334155

title: Time and Space Efficiency
text:
Practical optimisation strategy
A sensible workflow is:

write correct code first,
check that it produces the right results,
measure performance,
optimise the real bottlenecks.

Optimising too early can waste effort on parts of the code that are not important.

title: Time and Space Efficiency
text:
Why this matters in statistics
Statistical analysis often involves repeated tasks such as:

scanning large datasets,
computing summaries,
fitting models multiple times,
running simulations.

In these cases, choosing an efficient algorithm can make the difference between a script that finishes quickly and one that is too slow to use.

title: Time and Space Efficiency
text:
Summary
Efficiency is a combination of algorithmic thinking and practical measurement. Big O notation helps you compare approaches, but real performance also depends on the specific language, data size, and implementation.

title: Programming Best Practices
text: Programming best practices help make code easier to read, easier to maintain, and less likely to contain hidden bugs. They are especially useful in a statistics course, where reproducibility and clarity are critical.

title: Programming Best Practices
text: Programming best practices help make code easier to read, easier to maintain, and less likely to contain hidden bugs. They are especially useful in a statistics course, where reproducibility and clarity are critical.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Naming and readability
Choose clear names for variables, functions, and objects. Good names describe intent without forcing the reader to decode the logic.
Common naming conventions include:

snake_case (e.g. mean_score) in R and Python
camelCase (e.g. meanScore) in JavaScript and some other languages

Both are acceptable as long as you are consistent.

mean_score is better than x.
calculate_confidence_interval() is better than f().
student_age is better than sa.

Clear names make it easier to revisit code later and to share it with others.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Modular code
Break complex work into small reusable pieces. If a block of logic is repeated or conceptually separate, put it in a function.

A function should do one thing.
Functions make analysis scripts easier to test.
Modular code is easier to reuse in other analyses.

The reasoning for this was shown in the previous section on Abstraction, but the main purpose is compartmentalisation. By breaking code into modules, we can isolate specific functionality and test it independently. This also allows us to reuse code across different projects without copying and pasting alongside diagnosing issues. For example, if we have a function to calculate a z-score, we can use it in multiple places without rewriting the logic.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Comments and documentation
Comments should explain why a piece of code exists, not what the code literally does.

Use comments for intent, assumptions, and unusual decisions.
Keep comments up to date with the code.
Prefer short, clear explanations rather than long paragraphs.

Comments are essential for helping others, or your future self, understand the reasoning behind your code. They should provide context, not restate the code.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Reproducibility
A key goal in statistical programming is reproducibility.

Keep the analysis workflow in script or notebook form.
Avoid manual point-and-click steps when possible.
Save package versions or record the environment when needed.
Use version control such as git to track changes and collaborate safely.

This is done mostly through seed setting, allowing you to generate the same random numbers each time you run the code. By setting a seed, you ensure that your results can be replicated exactly, which is crucial for scientific research and for building trust in your analysis.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Testing and validation
Small checks inside your script can catch errors early.

Use stopifnot() to assert assumptions in R.
Check the shape and type of input data before using it.
Validate function outputs with simple examples.

Example:


Code
```{r}
x <- 7
stopifnot(is.numeric(x), length(x) > 0)
```

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Formatting and style
Consistent style helps a team read your code faster.

Use tools like styler for R or black for Python.
Keep functions short and focused.
Prefer clear code over clever one-liners.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Error handling and validation
When working with data, assume inputs may be imperfect.

Check data types before operating on them.
Handle missing values explicitly.
Use assertions or guards in functions to catch invalid inputs early.

This can be done through the use of tryCatch in R, which allows you to handle errors gracefully without crashing your entire script. By validating inputs and handling exceptions, you can make your code more robust and easier to debug when things go wrong. Alternatively, you can attempt to justify your decisions through the use of comments, which can help others understand the reasoning behind your error handling choices.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Performance awareness
Write code that is correct first, then consider whether it needs to be faster.

Use vectorised operations instead of explicit loops where possible.
Prefer built-in functions for data manipulation.
When necessary, use compiled code or packages designed for speed.

While performance can be important, it should not come at the cost of readability and correctness. Start by writing clear and correct code, and only optimise if you identify a bottleneck. In R, for example, using vectorised functions from packages like dplyr can often be much faster than writing explicit loops, while also being more readable. This will be focussed on more in the section on Time and Space Efficiency, but the key takeaway is to write code that is easy to understand first, and then optimise if needed.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Keep the story clear
A well-written analysis should tell a story.

Start with data preparation,
then move to modelling,
then finish with interpretation and diagnostics.

A clear narrative helps guide the reader through your thought process and makes the analysis easier to reproduce.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Collaboration and style
Good code is easier to share.

Use consistent formatting.
Keep functions short and focused.
Prefer clarity over cleverness.

Clean, consistent code is easier for others to read and modify.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Safe data handling
Handle data carefully and explicitly.

Validate input shapes and types.
Document assumptions about missing values.
Keep cleaning steps separate from modelling steps.

This reduces the risk of drawing conclusions from improperly prepared data.

title: Programming Best Practices
text:
Summary
Programming best practices are not rules for their own sake. They are habits that make statistical analysis more reliable, more transparent, and easier to maintain.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
Vectorisation means applying operations to whole vectors or arrays at once, rather than iterating element by element. In R, many built-in functions are vectorised.
Vectorised code is often faster because it lets the underlying implementation work in compiled code and avoid the overhead of many separate loop iterations.
In R we can measure time efficiency using the system.time() function.


Using a loop:


Code
```{r}
n <- 100000000
x <- rnorm(n)
y <- numeric(n)
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  y[i] <- x[i] ^ 2
}
system.time({
  n <- 100000000
  x <- rnorm(n)
  y <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    y[i] <- x[i] ^ 2
  }
})
```


   user  system elapsed 
   8.20    0.25    8.46 


Using vectorisation:


Code
```{r}
y <- x ^ 2
system.time({
  y <- x ^ 2
})
```


   user  system elapsed 
   0.19    0.08    0.26 


The vectorised version is shorter, easier to read, and typically much faster for large data. Remember that for small vectors, the difference may not be noticeable, but as the size of the data grows, the performance benefits of vectorisation become more pronounced. In this case we save about 0.1 seconds, which is a significant improvement when we scale to maybe 10 million or 100 million elements.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
When to use vectorisation
Vectorisation is a good first choice when:

the operation applies independently to each element,
the same transformation is used across a whole vector,
readability and speed are both important.

However, not every problem can be expressed cleanly in vectorised form. Complex algorithms or stateful loops may still require explicit iteration. The main benefit is that vectorised code is often more concise and can leverage optimized C or Fortran code under the hood, which can lead to significant performance improvements since it is compiled.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
Pre-allocate, don’t grow
When a loop is genuinely needed, the single most common performance mistake in R is growing an object one element at a time. Each time you write y <- c(y, value), R cannot extend the vector in place — it allocates a brand new, slightly larger vector and copies everything across. Doing that n times copies roughly 1 + 2 + ... + n elements, which is O(n^2) work hidden inside an innocent-looking loop.
The fix is to pre-allocate the result to its final size once, then fill it by index:


Code
```{r}
n <- 20000

# Slow: the vector is regrown on every iteration (O(n^2))
grow_vector <- function(n) {
  y <- numeric(0)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    y <- c(y, i^2)
  }
  y
}

# Fast: allocate once, then assign into existing slots (O(n))
prealloc_vector <- function(n) {
  y <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    y[i] <- i^2
  }
  y
}

system.time(grow_vector(n))
system.time(prealloc_vector(n))
```


   user  system elapsed 
   0.39    0.31    0.72 
   user  system elapsed 
   0.01    0.00    0.02 


Even at only 20,000 elements the difference is dramatic, and the gap widens quadratically as n grows. The same warning applies to rbind()-ing rows onto a data frame inside a loop — build a list and combine once at the end instead.






Tip



The hierarchy to remember: vectorise if you can → if you must loop, pre-allocate → never grow inside a loop.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
The apply family
R provides a family of functions that apply an operation across the elements of a vector, list, or the rows/columns of a matrix without an explicit for loop. They are not magically faster than a well-written loop, but they are concise, avoid the grow-in-a-loop trap automatically, and make intent clear.


Code
```{r}
# sapply: apply a function to each element and simplify to a vector
sapply(1:5, function(i) i^2)

# vapply: like sapply but you declare the return type — safer and slightly faster
vapply(1:5, function(i) i^2, numeric(1))

# lapply: returns a list (use when results are not all the same shape)
lapply(1:3, function(i) rnorm(i))
```


[1]  1  4  9 16 25
[1]  1  4  9 16 25
[[1]]
[1] -1.193181

[[2]]
[1] -0.7620886  0.6645333

[[3]]
[1] -1.698030 -1.839281 -1.490898


Use vapply() in production-style code: by stating the expected output type you catch errors early and avoid the surprises sapply() can produce when it cannot simplify the result.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
Prefer specialised built-ins
For common aggregations, R ships dedicated compiled functions that beat both loops and the apply family. If one exists for your task, use it:


Code
```{r}
m <- matrix(rnorm(1e6), nrow = 1000)

# Manual apply across rows
system.time(apply(m, 1, sum))

# Specialised, fully compiled equivalent
system.time(rowSums(m))
```


   user  system elapsed 
   0.02    0.00    0.01 
   user  system elapsed 
   0.01    0.00    0.00 


rowSums(), colMeans(), cumsum(), tabulate(), and which.max() are all examples of purpose-built functions that run almost entirely in C. Reaching for the specialised tool is usually both faster and clearer than assembling the same result yourself.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
Benchmarking properly
system.time() is fine for operations that take a noticeable fraction of a second, but for fast operations it is too coarse and noisy. The microbenchmark package runs each expression many times and reports a distribution, which is far more reliable for comparing close alternatives:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(microbenchmark)

x <- rnorm(1e5)

microbenchmark(
  loop      = { y <- numeric(length(x)); for (i in seq_along(x)) y[i] <- x[i]^2; y },
  vectorised = x^2,
  times = 100
)
```








Note



Always benchmark on data sizes close to your real problem. Vectorisation and compiled code win decisively on large inputs, but for a handful of elements the overhead of setting them up can make a plain loop just as fast — efficiency only matters where the data is big enough to feel it.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
R and compiled code
R is a high-level language, but much of its performance comes from compiled code under the hood. Many base functions and packages delegate work to C or C++.
This means the command you type in R may still run fast because it calls a compiled implementation.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
C++ code injection in R
When a calculation is very expensive, it can make sense to move the core work into compiled code.
Common approaches include:

the compiler package for bytecode compilation,
Rcpp for writing C++ code that interfaces with R,
sourceCpp() to compile and load C++ functions directly.

These techniques are usually reserved for performance-critical kernels rather than everyday data manipulation.

Example using Rcpp


Code
```{r}
library(Rcpp)
```


Warning: package 'Rcpp' was built under R version 4.4.3


Code
```{r}
cppFunction('NumericVector square_cpp(NumericVector x) {
  int n = x.size();
  NumericVector out(n);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    out[i] = x[i] * x[i];
  }
  return out;
}')

n <- 100000000
x <- rnorm(n)
y <- square_cpp(x)

system.time({
  y <- square_cpp(x)
})
```


   user  system elapsed 
   0.22    0.05    0.29 








Warning



This example requires a working C++ toolchain and the Rcpp package. If you do not have these installed, it will not work.








Note



Look at the fact that using Rcpp and vecorisation lead to almost the same speed. This is because Rcpp is compiled code, and vectorisation in R uses underlying C++ code since it is a very common operation but just hidden from you.


This example compiles the loop into native code, which can reduce overhead compared with an interpreted R loop.


Why this can help

The loop runs in compiled code rather than in R’s interpreter.
Memory management is still handled by R, but the inner computation is faster.
For large inputs or tight loops, compiled code can make a noticeable difference.



When to use it
Use C/C++ integration when you have:

a performance bottleneck in a tight loop,
a calculation that cannot be expressed cleanly with vectorised R functions,
a need for lower-level control over the computation.

If the operation can be expressed with existing vectorised R functions, that is usually the simpler and safer choice.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
Practical guidance

Start with readable R code.
Use vectorisation to avoid slow explicit loops.
Use compiled code only when you have identified a real bottleneck.
Prefer existing packages before writing your own C/C++ extension.

title: Efficiency in R
text:
Summary
Vectorisation and compiled code are two ways to make R faster. Vectorisation is the first tool to try, and C/C++ integration is a more advanced option for the heaviest computations.

title: Control Structures & Code Abstraction
text:
Abstraction is the process of hiding unnecessary detail so we can focus on the essential structure of a problem. In programming, this means solving a smaller, simpler problem first and then using that solution as a building block.
We use high-level languages because they let us write logic without thinking about hardware-level details. R and Python are far from the machine, so we can spend our energy on the algorithm rather than memory addresses.
Programming languages exist on a spectrum of abstraction. The level refers to how close the syntax is to human reasoning versus how close it is to the computer hardware.








Attribute
Low Level (Binary, Assembly)
Higher Level (R, Python)




Abstraction
Very low; interacts directly with memory/CPU
High; hides hardware complexities


Execution Time
Extremely fast; minimal translation required
Slower; requires interpretation or heavy runtime environments


Memory Management
Manual (allocating/freeing memory addresses)
Automatic


Development Time
Long; requires writing many lines of verbose code
Short; concise libraries solve problems instantly



From this it is evident that there is a trade off between efficiency and ease of use. Languages like C or C# are lower level than Python or R but are much more pedantic about small issues like semi-colons and declaring variable types.
For this course and for general understanding we will use very high level code syntax as a baseline and explore more efficient versions when needed (The lowest level versions I will leave up your interpretation). For this course examples will mostly be in R or Python since most uses of pseudo logic that people use is very similar to these programming languages.

title: Control Structures & Code Abstraction
text:
The Three Pillars of Logic
Every algorithm ever written relies on exactly three fundamental control structures to direct the flow of execution: Sequence, Selection, and Iteration.

title: Control Structures & Code Abstraction
text:
Sequence
Sequence means execution happens sequentially, one line after another, from top to bottom. The computer must completely finish the current statement before moving to the next one.
\[\text{Step 1: } x \leftarrow 5 \longrightarrow \text{Step 2: } y \leftarrow x + 10 \longrightarrow \text{Step 3: } \text{print}(y)\]

Example: Linear Execution in R


Code
```{r}
# Sequential operations
radius <- 7
area <- pi * radius^2
print(area)
```

text:
Visualising Control Structures
It can be difficult to see how these three pillars interact. The flowchart below shows how Sequence, Selection, and Iteration form the core workflow of any algorithm.





flowchart TD
    subgraph Sequence
    direction TB
    A[Step 1] --> B[Step 2] --> C[Step 3]
    end

title: Control Structures & Code Abstraction
text:
Putting It All Together
In practice, algorithms rarely use just one of these structures. They are nested. Here is a classic statistical example: simulating a coin flip to count how many heads we get in 10 flips.

Iteration: We need to flip the coin 10 times.
Sequence: In each flip, we generate a random number, check it, and update our count.
Selection: We only add to our count if the result is a Head.

# SEQUENCE: Initialise our starting variables
nFlips <- 10
heads <- 0

# ITERATION: Run the process 10 times
for (i in 1:nFlips) {

  # SEQUENCE: Generate a random number (0 or 1)
  flip <- sample(0:1, 1)

  # SELECTION: Check if it is a 1 (Head)
  if (flip == 1) {
    heads <- heads + 1
  }
}

# SEQUENCE: Print final result
print(paste("Total Heads:", heads))

title: Report Structure
text:
There are several acceptable ways to structure a statistical report. The structure outlined below is an example of one that does well in terms of clarity, readability, and reproducibility, and closely follows conventions used in professional statistical writing. Though, feel free to diverge from this structure if you feel it necessary.
The report is composed of a sequence of components, listed below in the order in which they should appear. Longer reports will usually benefit from being divided explicitly into sections, while very short reports may adopt a simplified version of this structure. Nevertheless, the logical separation of components should always be respected.
A narrative approach should be avoided. Reports written as a chronological account of actions (for example, “First I did this, then I did that”) are difficult to follow and obscure the logical structure of the analysis. Statistical reports are not diaries of activity; they are structured arguments supported by data.

Nevertheless, the logical separation of components should always be respected.
A narrative approach should be avoided. Reports written as a chronological account of actions (for example, “First I did this, then I did that”) are difficult to follow and obscure the logical structure of the analysis. Statistical reports are not diaries of activity; they are structured arguments supported by data.

title: Report Structure
text:
Title
Every statistical report requires a title. In most cases, this should appear on a separate title page, which should also include:

the author’s name,
institutional affiliation (department or organisation),
the date of submission.

However, for coursework your student ID number, Module code, and Assignment number should suffice.
Now, back to professional reports. The title should be short, specific, and informative. Its purpose is to tell the reader what the report is about before they read a single paragraph. Vague titles such as “The statistical analysis of two data sets” fail to identify either the problem or the context.
Effective titles typically indicate:

the subject or phenomenon under study,
the population or data source,
sometimes (but not always) the general type of analysis.

For Example:

“A Hybrid Approach to Financial Markets: Integrating SPDEs and Bayesian Neural Networks”
“Lifetime earnings and the Vietnam era draft lottery: evidence from Social Security administrative records”
“Using empirical Bayes techniques in the law school validity studies”

title: Report Structure
text:
Summary / Abstract
A brief summary or abstract should follow the title. You will most likely never need to submit this in any of your coursework, however it is convention in professional works. This section should be concise, ideally no longer than half a page, and is often the most widely read part of the report (turns out researchers are also lazy!).
The abstract should provide a detailed overview of:

the problem being addressed,
what was done,
the main conclusions reached.

The abstract should be written in plain language, avoiding symbols, equations, and numerical detail wherever possible. Technical terms should only be used if they are both unavoidable and widely understood by the intended audience. The purpose of the abstract is not to convince the reader of technical correctness, but to allow them to decide whether the report is relevant and worth reading.
Here is an excellent example of a concise, well-structured technical abstract aimed at a specialist audience:
“The analysis of censored failure times is considered. It is assumed that on each individual are available values of one or more explanatory variables. The hazard function (age-specific failure rate) is taken to be a function of the explanatory variables and unknown regression coefficients multiplied by an arbitrary and unknown function of time. A conditional likelihood is obtained, leading to inferences about the unknown regression coefficients. Some generalizations are outlined.” - Cox D. R. ‘Regression Models and Life-Tables.’ Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B (Methodological), vol. 34, no. 2, 1972.

title: Report Structure
text:
Introduction
The introduction places the analysis in context. It should describe the background to the problem and explain why the investigation is of interest.
Typically, the introduction includes:

a description of the general setting,
an outline of the available data,
how and why the data were collected,
the aims and objectives of the investigation.

The introduction may be viewed as an expanded version of the abstract, but with greater detail and motivation. It should also give a brief indication of the statistical methods employed, without entering into technical detail. As a general guideline, the introduction should not exceed two pages in length. Importantly, it should not contain results or conclusions, which belong in later sections.

title: Report Structure
text:
Methods
The methods section describes how the analysis was carried out, in sufficient detail for it to be replicated by a reader of comparable background (for example, a student at the same academic level). This section should include:

a clear description of the analytical strategy,
any assumptions made,
the statistical models, tests, or procedures used,
any theoretical background necessary to understand the analysis.

Deciding how much detail to include is often difficult. A useful guiding principle is reproducibility: the reader should be able to repeat the analysis using the information provided. Very detailed material (like derivations, extra plots, extra tables, etc.) may be placed in one or more appendices.

Structure of the Methods Section
The methods section often benefits from being divided into subsections, for example:

A preliminary analysis (a more formal version of EDA), using graphical methods and simple descriptive statistics.
A full-scale analysis, employing more rigorous statistical techniques.

The full-scale analysis may itself be divided into:

(a) Methodology: a description or development of the statistical tools to be used,
(b) Implementation: the application of these tools to the data.

Subsection (a) is typically the most technical part of the report. Mathematical notation should be used where appropriate, but every symbol must be explicitly defined. An expression containing undefined symbols is meaningless, regardless of its mathematical sophistication. Similarly, pages of algebra or statistical derivation are of no value if the notation is unclear or inconsistent.
In subsection (b), the analysis should be described clearly and systematically, so that a reader could reproduce the results step by step.

title: Report Structure
text:
Results, Conclusions, and Recommendations
This section presents the main findings of the analysis and the conclusions drawn from them. Primary results should be presented clearly and concisely. Subsidiary results may be included if they support the main conclusions and do not interrupt the flow of the presentation. Otherwise, they may be:

moved to an appendix,
integrated into the methods section,
or presented in a separate results subsection.

Conclusions should be expressed in language accessible to a non-statistician and should make sense even if the reader has not read the detailed statistical analysis. Whenever possible, conclusions should be framed in the context of the original problem or experiment.
Recommendations, if appropriate, should follow naturally from the conclusions and be proportionate to the strength of the evidence.

title: Report Structure
text:
General Discussion
The general discussion places the results in a broader context.
This may include:

comparison with previous studies or related work,
discussion of how successfully the original aims were achieved,
limitations of the data or methods,
reflections on alternative approaches.

In applied work, it is particularly important to acknowledge potential problems with the data, such as measurement error or poor experimental design. In some reports, this discussion may be integrated into the introduction rather than appearing as a separate section. Nevertheless, both approaches allow for more honest scientific communication and allow others to validate your work.

title: Report Structure
text:
References
Any books, articles, or external sources referred to in the report must be cited. There are countably infinite (slight exaggeration) citation styles that exist and you must research what they are depending on who you are writing a report for. Despite this there are basic elements that all formats share.
For journal articles, references should include:

author(s),
year of publication,
title of the article,
journal name,
volume number,
page range.

For books, references should include:

author(s),
year of publication,
title (in italics),
publisher,
place of publication.

Consistency of style is essential, so if you choose one style, stick with it!

title: Report Structure
text:
Appendix
Material that does not fit naturally into the main body of the report, but cannot reasonably be omitted, should be placed in an appendix. Typical appendix material includes:

lengthy derivations,
supplementary tables,
additional figures,
extended methodological details.

However, excessive reliance on appendices should be avoided. If the appendices dominate the report, readability suffers. The main text should always remain the primary method for communication!!!

title: How to Report Statistical Results
text:
The presentation of a statistical report is not just cosmetic. Clear, well-organised presentation is important for communicating results accurately and efficiently. A well-presented report allows the reader to focus on the statistical content rather than expending effort deciphering layout, notation, or formatting.
Reports should therefore be neat, clean, legible, and logically organised. RMarkdown makes it straightforward to produce professional-quality documents.

title: How to Report Statistical Results
section: Reporting Numerical Values and Choosing Suitable Precision
text:
Reporting Numerical Values and Choosing Suitable Precision
Numerical precision should reflect the accuracy of the data and the purpose of the analysis, not the computing power used to generate the results.
As a general rule: * do not report more decimal places than are scientifically meaningful, * ensure consistency across tables and figures, * avoid implying spurious accuracy.
For example: * reporting a mean as 12.347891 is almost never appropriate, * reporting 12.3 or 12.35 may be appropriate depending on context.
As another example, P-values should typically be reported to two or three significant figures (e.g. p = 0.032), except when extremely small (e.g. p < 0.001).

title: How to Report Statistical Results
text:
Figures, Plots, and Diagrams
Figures, plots, and diagrams should:

be numbered sequentially,
have clear titles and captions,
be referred to explicitly in the text,
be placed close to the point where they are discussed.

Axes must be clearly labelled, units indicated, and scales chosen sensibly. Furthermore, a statistical report should be easy to navigate. Section headings, numbering, and figure references act as signposts that guide the reader through the argument.
For more details on data visualisation, refer to the pages dedicated to it through the navigation menu to the left of the webpage.

title: How to Report Statistical Results
text:
Tables
Tables are often the most effective way to present numerical summaries, provided they are well constructed. Every table should:

have a table number,
have a clear title or caption,
include labelled rows and columns,
state units where relevant,
align numerical values correctly (typically on the decimal point).

Tables should not duplicate information already presented clearly in figures. Each table should serve a distinct purpose.

title: How to Report Statistical Results
section: Constructing Tables in R Using dplyr, kable, and kableExtra
text:
Constructing Tables in R Using dplyr, kable, and kableExtra
In modern statistical reporting, tables are generated directly from data using reproducible code. In R, this workflow typically combines:

dplyr for data manipulation,
knitr::kable() for table creation,
kableExtra for professional formatting.

We illustrate this workflow using the penguins dataset from the palmerpenguins package.


Preparing Data with dplyr
The penguins dataset contains measurements on three penguin species collected in Antarctica. We begin by loading the data and performing basic preparation.


Code
library(dplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)

data(penguins)


As with most real datasets, penguins contains missing values. For descriptive tables, it is important to handle these explicitly rather than silently ignoring them.
We construct a Table 1–style summary, stratified by species.


Code
summ <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(bill_length_mm),
         !is.na(body_mass_g)) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm),
    sd_bill_length = sd(bill_length_mm),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
    sd_body_mass = sd(body_mass_g)
  )

summ


# A tibble: 3 × 6
  species       n mean_bill_length sd_bill_length mean_body_mass sd_body_mass
  <fct>     <int>            <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>        <dbl>
1 Adelie      151             38.8           2.66          3701.         459.
2 Chinstrap    68             48.8           3.34          3733.         384.
3 Gentoo      123             47.5           3.08          5076.         504.


This table contains only descriptive statistics and provides an overview of the dataset. No hypothesis tests or p-values are included.



Basic Tables with kable
The kable() function converts a data frame into a clean, professional table.


Code
library(knitr)

kable(
  summ,
  caption = "Table 1: Descriptive statistics of penguin characteristics by species",
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c(
    "Species",
    "Sample size",
    "Mean bill length (mm)",
    "SD bill length (mm)",
    "Mean body mass (g)",
    "SD body mass (g)"
  )
)

Enhancing Tables with kableExtra
For more polished presentation, kableExtra provides tools for alignment, grouping, and emphasis.


Code
library(kableExtra)

kable(

You can find more options to make your tables more interesting and informative in the documentation of kableExtra.



Common Enhancements and When to Use Them
Some frequently used kableExtra features include:

Row emphasis Useful for highlighting reference groups or totals.
row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
Footnotes Great when clarifying missing data, transformations, or units.
footnote(
  general = "Values are means with standard deviations in parentheses."
)
Controlled column width Helps prevent overly wide tables in HTML or PDF output.
column_spec(2:6, width = "3cm")

These tools should be used sparingly. Tables should remain clear without relying on heavy styling.


Referencing Tables in the Text
Every table must be referenced explicitly. For example:

“Table 1 summarises key morphological characteristics of the penguins by species.”

A table that is not discussed does not contribute to the report and should be removed.

title: How to Report Statistical Results
text:
Computer Output
Raw computer output is rarely suitable for direct inclusion in a report, unless asked for. Output should be:

edited,
selectively included,
formatted consistently with the rest of the document.

The key idea is that relevant results should be extracted, summarised, and presented clearly in tables or figures.
Unedited output dumps obscure key findings and signal a lack of engagement with the analysis.
You can choose to place all of your code at the end of your RMarkdown report in an Appendix using the two following chunks:


Code
```{r}
##| Place this one at the start of your RMarkdown file, after the YAML block

# knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE,
#                      message=FALSE,
#                      out.width = "80%",
#                      fig.align = "center")
#library(tidyverse)
#library(ggplot2)
#library(knitr)
#library(tinytex)
#library(MASS)
#...
# Other Libraries
```


Now for a code chunk that will print all of the code in your RMD file into one continuous code block:


Code
##| Place this one at the end of your RMarkdown file and include the following in your chunk options for this R chunk:

# ref.label=knitr::all_labels(),

# I haven't included it since it would re-print all of the code above here.


While these two chunks will not explicitly create an appendix, they will place all of the code present in the respective RMarkdown (.Rmd) file at the end of the knitted output. You can then insert markdown text above the last block to create an appendix.

title: English and Style
text:
Clear and precise use of English is half of what makes up statistical writing. The primary purpose of writing, as with speaking, is communication. This becomes especially important when explaining abstract or technically demanding ideas, which is what the job of a statistician is. Well-written English is easy to read and understand; poorly written English quickly obscures meaning and can render an otherwise sound analysis unintelligible.
A common and easily corrected weakness in project reports is the failure to construct proper sentences. Every sentence should contain a clear main verb, and a useful first check when proofreading is to ask whether this verb can be identified. A more subtle and frequent problem occurs when the writer unconsciously assumes that the reader is following an unstated line of reasoning. Readers are often presumed to know which variables are under discussion, what quantities are being held fixed, and what is allowed to vary, even though none of this has been explicitly stated. Sentences may appear correct on first reading but reveal their ambiguity or emptiness once one attempts to interpret their precise meaning.
Improving writing quality is an acquired skill that requires sustained effort. As with learning to drive, some people may find it easier than others, but everyone can improve through practice. While many guides to good writing exist, one of the most effective ways to develop a clear style is to read widely and attentively, observing how skilled writers structure arguments and convey complex ideas.


Several practical rules can greatly improve clarity and readability:

Be concise and precise. Prefer shorter, simpler words where they convey the same meaning. Avoid unnecessary digressions: material that does not fit naturally under a section heading should be moved elsewhere or omitted entirely.
Avoid the personal pronoun “I”. Scientific and statistical writing is usually impersonal. Passive constructions or neutral phrasing are generally preferable, for example: “A regression analysis was carried out” rather than “I carried out a regression analysis”.
Use tenses consistently. The usual convention is to use the past tense when describing what was done (for example, methods and data collection, as in “A regression analysis was carried out”), and the present tense when stating results and conclusions (e.g. “The analysis shows that…”).
Ensure correct spelling. If uncertain about a word, consult a reliable dictionary or use a spell-checker. Persistent spelling errors distract the reader and undermine confidence in the work.
Use words accurately. Similar-sounding terms may have distinct meanings; for example, “trend” and “tendency” are not interchangeable. The word “significant” should be used only in its statistical sense.
Write complete, grammatical sentences. Telegraphic fragments such as “A standard analysis is possible. By regression.” are unacceptable. Mathematical and statistical writing follows the same grammatical rules as ordinary English.
Treat “data” as a plural noun. The correct form is “data are…”, since “data” is the plural of “datum”.

Developing a clear and readable style does not come naturally to many mathematicians and statisticians, but it is a worthwhile goal. Reading good prose, practising writing, and critically revising one’s own work are the most reliable ways to improve.
