title: Poisson Regression (Count Data)
text: The second great non-normal response is the count: a non-negative integer \(0, 1, 2, \dots\) — accidents per junction, emails per hour, warp breaks per loom. The natural model is Poisson regression, the Poisson-distribution, log-link member of the GLM family. It introduces one genuinely new practical concern that dominates real count analysis: overdispersion.

title: Poisson Regression (Count Data)
text:
Fix 1 — quasi-Poisson
The lightest fix keeps the Poisson mean model but lets the variance be \(\phi\mu\) for an estimated dispersion parameter \(\phi\), which simply inflates the standard errors to honest sizes. Change one word: family = quasipoisson.


Code
```{r}
modelQuasi <- glm(breaks ~ wool + tension, data = warpbreaks, family = quasipoisson)
# Same coefficients as before, but wider (more honest) standard errors
summary(modelQuasi)$coefficients
```


              Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  3.6919631 0.09374352 39.383662 2.635587e-39
woolB       -0.2059884 0.10646089 -1.934874 5.867292e-02
tensionM    -0.3213204 0.12440965 -2.582761 1.277482e-02
tensionH    -0.5184885 0.13203462 -3.926913 2.639908e-04


The point estimates are unchanged; the standard errors grow to reflect the true variability.

title: Poisson Regression (Count Data)
text:
Fix 2 — the negative binomial
A fuller fix replaces the distribution entirely with the negative binomial, which has a separate parameter allowing the variance to exceed the mean, \(\text{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta\). It is the count analogue of “the model itself was wrong, not just its error bars,” and is fitted with glm.nb from the MASS package.


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(MASS)
modelNB <- glm.nb(breaks ~ wool + tension, data = warpbreaks)
AIC(model, modelNB)        # lower AIC = better fit; the NB usually wins when overdispersed
```








TipGoing further 🚀



Two more count complications worth knowing. Excess zeros — far more zero counts than any Poisson or NB predicts (e.g. number of fish caught, where many visitors never fish) — are handled by zero-inflated or hurdle models in the pscl package (zeroinfl, hurdle). And the dispersion check above can be automated with performance::check_overdispersion(), which runs a formal test rather than eyeballing the ratio.

title: Introduction to Generalised Linear Models
text:
The Linear modelling section fitted a straight-line relationship \(Y = X\beta + \epsilon\) and leaned on four assumptions — linearity, constant variance, independence and normal errors. That model is superb when the response is a continuous, unbounded quantity (height, burn time, river length). But a great deal of real data is not like that: a coin lands heads or tails, a hospital records a count of admissions, a survey returns a proportion. Forcing a linear model onto such data breaks its assumptions and produces nonsense — negative counts, predicted probabilities above 1, wildly wrong uncertainty.
Generalised linear models (GLMs) are the elegant fix. They keep everything good about the linear model — a linear combination of predictors — but generalise it in two precise ways so it can handle binary, count, and other non-normal responses. This section builds them from the linear model you already know and the maximum-likelihood machinery from the Frequentist Statistics section.





flowchart LR
  LM["Linear model<br/>continuous, normal response<br/>Y = Xβ + ε"] --> G["Generalise in two ways"]
  G --> R["1. Let Y follow a<br/>different distribution<br/>(binomial, Poisson, …)"]
  G --> L["2. Connect the mean to Xβ<br/>through a link function"]
  R --> GLM["Generalised linear model"]
  L --> GLM







Why the linear model is not enough
Consider three responses a statistician meets constantly:

Binary — did the patient survive (1) or not (0)? A linear model can predict \(1.4\) or \(-0.2\), neither of which is a valid probability.
Counts — how many emails arrived this hour? Counts are non-negative integers; a straight line happily predicts \(-3\) emails, and the variance of counts grows with the mean, violating constant variance.
Proportions — what fraction of seeds germinated? Bounded in \([0,1]\), with variance that shrinks near the boundaries.

In every case two linear-model assumptions fail at once: the response is not normal, and its variance is not constant. We could try transforming \(Y\), but that is a blunt instrument — you cannot take the log of a zero count, and modelling \(\log Y\) changes the question. GLMs solve the problem at the source.






NoteIn a nutshell: when do I reach for a GLM?



Look at your response variable. If it is a continuous measurement that can sensibly be any real number, an ordinary linear model is fine. If it is yes/no, a count, a proportion, or strictly positive and skewed, a linear model will misbehave and you want a GLM with the matching distribution.




The three components of a GLM
Every GLM is built from exactly three pieces. Learn these and you can read any GLM — logistic, Poisson, or otherwise — off a single template.





flowchart TD
  A["<b>1. Random component</b><br/>the distribution of Y<br/>(Normal, Binomial, Poisson, …)<br/>with mean μ = E[Y]"]
  B["<b>2. Systematic component</b><br/>the linear predictor<br/>η = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … = Xβ"]
  C["<b>3. Link function</b><br/>g(μ) = η<br/>connects the mean to the predictor"]
  B --> C
  C --> A







The random component — the probability distribution assumed for the response \(Y\). For a linear model this is the Normal; for binary data it is the Bernoulli/Binomial; for counts the Poisson. All the usual choices belong to a family (the exponential family) that makes the maths work out cleanly, but you rarely need that detail to use a GLM.
The systematic component — the linear predictor \(\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p = X\beta\). This is exactly the right-hand side of the linear model; it is still linear in the parameters, so everything you learned about design matrices and coefficients carries over.
The link function \(g\) — the new ingredient. Instead of equating the mean directly to the linear predictor, we connect them through an invertible function: \(g(\mu) = \eta\), equivalently \(\mu = g^{-1}(\eta)\). The link is what keeps the mean inside its natural range.



The link function: the key new idea
Why not just set \(\mu = X\beta\) as in a linear model? Because the linear predictor \(\eta = X\beta\) can be any real number — but the mean of the response often cannot. A probability must lie in \([0,1]\); a Poisson rate must be positive. The link function is a translator between the unbounded world of \(X\beta\) and the constrained world of \(\mu\).
Take binary data. The mean of a 0/1 response is a probability \(p \in [0,1]\). The logit link \[
g(p) = \log\!\frac{p}{1-p} = \eta
\] maps a probability in \([0,1]\) to a log-odds in \((-\infty, \infty)\), so the linear predictor is free to roam while the back-transformed prediction \(p = g^{-1}(\eta) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}\) is guaranteed to stay a valid probability. For counts, the log link \(g(\mu) = \log\mu = \eta\) does the same job: \(\mu = e^{\eta}\) is always positive.






NoteIn a nutshell: what the link is for



The link function exists so the model can never make an impossible prediction. We do the linear algebra on a scale where any number is allowed (the link scale, \(\eta = X\beta\)), then squash the answer back into the response’s legal range (probabilities into \([0,1]\), rates into the positives). Fit on the link scale; interpret on the response scale.




The common GLMs at a glance
Three choices — distribution, plus its standard (“canonical”) link — cover the vast majority of practice. Notice the first row is just the ordinary linear model: the linear model is the special case of a GLM with a Normal response and an identity link.










Response type
Distribution
Canonical link
family = in R
Section page

gaussian
(the Linear modelling section)

(brief mention)





How a GLM is fitted
A linear model has a tidy closed-form solution (least squares). A GLM usually does not — but we already have the tool to fit it: maximum likelihood, from the Frequentist section. We write down the likelihood implied by the chosen distribution, with the mean of each observation tied to its linear predictor through the link, and find the \(\hat\beta\) that maximises it.
Because the score equations have no closed form, R solves them numerically with an algorithm called iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) — in effect, repeatedly fitting a weighted linear model until the estimates stop changing. You never run it by hand: the single function glm() does everything, and its output deliberately mirrors lm().


Code
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# A linear model IS a GLM — fitting mtcars mpg ~ wt both ways gives identical coefficients
linModel <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
glmModel <- glm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars, family = gaussian)   # Normal + identity link

rbind(lm  = coef(linModel),
      glm = coef(glmModel))
```


    (Intercept)        wt
lm     37.28513 -5.344472
glm    37.28513 -5.344472


The two rows are identical — confirming that glm() with family = gaussian is ordinary linear regression. Switching family to binomial or poisson is all it takes to move to logistic or Poisson regression, which the next pages do in detail.






TipGoing further 🚀



The exponential family is the formal glue here: every distribution in the table writes its density in a common form, which is exactly what guarantees the score has mean zero and makes IRLS work. The same framework extends well beyond this section — to quasi-likelihood (modelling the mean–variance relationship without a full distribution), mgcv::gam() for generalised additive models (smooth, non-linear predictors), and lme4::glmer() for generalised linear mixed models with random effects. All of them keep the three-component skeleton you have just learned.




Where this section is going
We now turn the template into working models, one distribution at a time.


Logistic regression — binary and proportion data with the logit link; odds, odds ratios, and turning predictions into classifications.
Poisson regression — count data with the log link; rate ratios, offsets, and the ever-present problem of overdispersion (and its fix, the negative binomial).
Diagnostics and inference for GLMs — deviance, residuals, likelihood-ratio tests, AIC, and how to check a GLM actually fits.
Check your understanding — fit and interpret GLMs yourself.


The thread throughout: a GLM is the linear model you already know, wearing a distribution and a link so it can speak the language of binary, count and bounded data.

title: Check Your Understanding
text:
Time to fit GLMs yourself. Each question uses a dataset built into R, so you can run everything without downloading anything. Attempt each part before opening the answer — the solutions are hidden in the collapsible boxes.

Question 1 — Logistic regression
R’s mtcars records, for 32 cars, whether the engine is V-shaped (vs = 0) or straight (vs = 1), along with fuel economy mpg.

Fit a logistic regression predicting vs from mpg. Is higher fuel economy associated with higher or lower odds of a straight engine?
Report the odds ratio for mpg and explain what it means.
Predict the probability that a car doing 25 mpg has a straight engine.







NoteShow answer






```{r}
#| code-fold: false
q1 <- glm(vs ~ mpg, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
coef(summary(q1))
```

              Estimate Std. Error   z value    Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -8.8330726   3.162274 -2.793266 0.005217877
mpg          0.4304135   0.158422  2.716880 0.006590045


(a) The mpg coefficient is positive, so higher fuel economy is associated with higher log-odds — and therefore higher odds and probability — of a straight engine.
(b) The odds ratio is the exponentiated coefficient:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
exp(coef(q1))["mpg"]
```

     mpg 
1.537893 


Each extra 1 mpg multiplies the odds of a straight engine by this factor (greater than 1 → the odds increase with mpg).
(c) Predict on the response scale to get a probability:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
predict(q1, newdata = data.frame(mpg = 25), type = "response")
```

        1 
0.8729464 







Question 2 — Poisson regression
R’s InsectSprays gives the count of insects surviving on agricultural units treated with one of six sprays (spray, levels A–F).

Fit a Poisson regression of count on spray. Which spray is the baseline (reference) level?
Interpret the rate ratio for spray C relative to the baseline.
Check the model for overdispersion.







NoteShow answer






```{r}
#| code-fold: false
q2 <- glm(count ~ spray, data = InsectSprays, family = poisson)
exp(coef(q2))
```

(Intercept)      sprayB      sprayC      sprayD      sprayE      sprayF 
 14.5000000   1.0574713   0.1436782   0.3390805   0.2413793   1.1494253 


(a) Factor levels are coded alphabetically, so spray A is the baseline — it is absorbed into the intercept, and every other coefficient is relative to it.
(b) The rate ratio for sprayC is well below 1: spray C produces only that fraction of spray A’s insect count — a large reduction. (For example, a rate ratio of \(0.1\) means about 90% fewer insects than spray A.)
(c) Compare the residual deviance to its degrees of freedom, or estimate the dispersion from the Pearson residuals:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
c(ratio = q2$deviance / q2$df.residual,
  dispersion = sum(residuals(q2, type = "pearson")^2) / q2$df.residual)
```

     ratio dispersion 
  1.489828   1.507713 


Both are close to 1, so this Poisson model shows no serious overdispersion — unusually well-behaved for real count data. (Had they been well above 1, you would switch to quasipoisson or MASS::glm.nb.)





Question 3 — Choosing the right GLM
No code — just identify, for each response variable, the distribution and link you would use (i.e. what to put in family =).

Whether a customer churns (leaves) or not, from their usage.
The number of goals a football team scores in a match, from possession statistics.
The proportion of defective items in batches of 100, from the production line used.

Note that (c) is still binomial — a proportion is just a count of successes out of a known number of trials, so logistic regression handles it once you supply the successes and failures as two columns.





Question 4 — Reading a fitted model
The model below is fitted for you. Without running anything new, answer from the output:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
q4 <- glm(am ~ hp, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
exp(cbind(oddsRatio = coef(q4), confint(q4)))
```

Waiting for profiling to be done...


            oddsRatio     2.5 %    97.5 %
(Intercept) 2.1740973 0.3782630 14.669845
hp          0.9919157 0.9788241  1.002968



Does higher horsepower raise or lower the odds of a manual gearbox (am = 1)?
Does the 95% confidence interval for the hp odds ratio include 1, and why does that matter?







NoteShow answer





(a) The hp odds ratio is below 1, so higher horsepower is associated with lower odds of a manual gearbox (more powerful cars in this data tend to be automatics).
(b) Look at whether the hp row’s lower and upper bounds straddle 1. An odds ratio of 1 means “no effect,” so if the interval includes 1 the effect is not statistically clear at the 5% level; if it lies entirely below 1, the negative association is significant. (This is the odds-scale version of “does the coefficient’s confidence interval contain zero?” — recall that odds ratio \(=1\) corresponds to log-odds coefficient \(=0\).)




If you can fit each model, exponentiate the coefficients into odds or rate ratios, turn predictions into probabilities, and check for overdispersion, you have the working toolkit of generalised linear models. From here, the natural next steps are the broader model families flagged in the Going further boxes — mixed models, GAMs, and the machine-learning methods of later sections.

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
text:
The previous page built confidence intervals from clean asymptotic formulas. But those formulas only exist when the model is tractable — when we can write the answer down by hand. This page is about everything else: what to do when the algebra runs out and we must let the computer do the work through simulation.
The guiding idea is simple. The frequentist definition of probability imagines repeating the experiment many times. We can never do that in the real world — but on a computer we can. Simulation makes the imaginary repetitions real.
flowchart TD
  Q["I have an estimate θ̂.<br/>How do I quantify its uncertainty?"]
  Q --> T{"Is the problem tractable?<br/>(closed-form SE,<br/>known sampling distribution)"}
  T -->|"Yes"| A["Use the formula<br/>(Wald / likelihood-ratio CI<br/>from the previous page)"]
  T -->|"No"| S["Simulate:<br/>Monte Carlo / bootstrap"]
crumbs: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
text:
Parametric bootstrap
If we believe the model, we generate many fake data sets from the fitted model, re-estimate on each, and read off the variability directly. This works even when no standard-error formula exists.
crumbs: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
text:
Nonparametric bootstrap
If we do not want to lean on the parametric model, we instead resample the observed data with replacement to form many pseudo-samples. Each resample mimics “drawing a fresh data set,” and re-estimating on each reveals how much the estimate would wobble. This needs almost no theory at all — only the data.






NoteIn a nutshell: why sampling with replacement works



Resampling with replacement (sample(x, replace = TRUE)) pretends our sample is the whole population and draws a brand-new data set from it. Because each draw can repeat earlier values, no two resamples are identical — so they stand in for the fresh data sets we wish we could collect but cannot.
crumbs: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
text:
Parametric bootstrap (trust the exponential model)


Code
```{r}
B <- 5000
psiPar <- numeric(B)
for (b in 1:B) {
  xStar <- rexp(n, rate = lamHat)   # new data FROM the fitted model
  lamStar <- 1 / mean(xStar)
  psiPar[b] <- exp(-lamStar * t)
}

ciPar <- quantile(psiPar, c(0.025, 0.975))
c(estimate = psiHat, se = sd(psiPar), ciPar)
```


  estimate         se       2.5%      97.5% 
0.28223581 0.04005689 0.20111916 0.35618013
crumbs: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
text:
Nonparametric bootstrap (let the data speak)


Code
```{r}
psiNp <- numeric(B)
for (b in 1:B) {
  xStar <- sample(x, size = n, replace = TRUE)  # resample the DATA
  lamStar <- 1 / mean(xStar)
  psiNp[b] <- exp(-lamStar * t)
}

ciNp <- quantile(psiNp, c(0.025, 0.975))
c(estimate = psiHat, se = sd(psiNp), ciNp)
```


  estimate         se       2.5%      97.5% 
0.28223581 0.05410211 0.17335219 0.38532988 


Both bootstraps give us a standard error and a confidence interval for \(\psi\) without ever differentiating anything. The picture below shows the simulated distribution of \(\hat\psi\) — its spread is the uncertainty we could not derive by hand.


Code
```{r}
#| fig-align: center

hist(psiPar, breaks = 40, col = "lightsteelblue", border = "white",
     main = expression(paste("Bootstrap distribution of  ", hat(psi))),
     xlab = expression(hat(psi)))
abline(v = psiHat, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(v = ciPar, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = exp(-trueLam * t), col = "black", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2, 3),
       col = c("firebrick", "darkgreen", "black"),
       legend = c("estimate", "95% CI", "true value"))
```
crumbs: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
section: How the likelihood itself wobbles under resampling
text:
How the likelihood itself wobbles under resampling
The histogram above summarises the resampling by a single number per resample (\(\hat\psi\)). It is more revealing to watch the whole log-likelihood function move as we resample. Each bootstrap data set produces its own log-likelihood curve in \(\lambda\), peaking at its own MLE — yet the truth is fixed (the red line). This is the frequentist picture made visible: the data is random, the parameter is not.
For the exponential model the log-likelihood is \(\ell(\lambda) = n\log\lambda - \lambda\sum_i x_i\). We overlay this curve for many resampled data sets:


Code
```{r}
#| fig-align: center

grid <- seq(0.25, 0.85, length.out = 400)

# Exponential log-likelihood for a given data vector
llExp <- function(lambda, data) {
  length(data) * log(lambda) - lambda * sum(data)
}

# Set up an empty plot
plot(NA, xlim = range(grid), ylim = c(-180, -120),
     xlab = expression(lambda),
     ylab = expression(paste("log-likelihood  ", ell(lambda))),
     main = "Log-likelihood across 200 resamples (truth fixed in red)")

# One translucent log-likelihood curve per resample
for (b in 1:200) {
  xStar <- sample(x, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  lines(grid, llExp(grid, xStar),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.12))
}

# The fixed truth: a single red vertical line that does NOT move
abline(v = trueLam, col = "red", lwd = 3)

legend("bottomright", bty = "n",
       lwd = c(2, 3), col = c("steelblue", "red"),
       legend = c("resampled log-likelihoods", expression(paste("true  ", lambda))))
```









Notice that the peaks scatter left and right of the red line — each resample’s MLE misses the truth by a little, in a different direction — but they cluster around it. That scatter of peaks is precisely the sampling variability the bootstrap is estimating; the standard error we computed above is just a numerical summary of how far these curves’ maxima typically stray from the fixed truth.






TipGoing further 🚀



Hand-written bootstrap loops are great for understanding, but the boot package does it properly — including the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) interval, which corrects the naive percentile interval for skew and bias:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(boot)
psiFun <- function(data, idx) exp(-(1 / mean(data[idx])) * t)
bt <- boot(x, psiFun, R = 5000)
boot.ci(bt, type = "bca")
```


For a single proportion near the boundary (where the Wald interval misbehaves badly, as the coverage study below shows), binom::binom.confint offers the Wilson and Agresti–Coull intervals, which keep their coverage where Wald fails:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(binom)
binom.confint(x = 3, n = 15, methods = c("wilson", "agresti-coull", "asymptotic"))
```

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
text:
Example: fitting a Gamma distribution
The Gamma distribution has two parameters — a shape \(\alpha\) and a rate \(\beta\) — and its MLEs have no closed form: the shape equation involves the digamma function and must be solved numerically. This makes it a perfect two-parameter optim example.


Code
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

set.seed(123)

# "Unknown" truth and observed data
trueShape <- 2.5
trueRate  <- 1.5
n <- 300
x <- rgamma(n, shape = trueShape, rate = trueRate)

# Negative log-likelihood as a function of the parameter VECTOR theta = (shape, rate)
nll <- function(theta) {
  shape <- theta[1]
  rate  <- theta[2]
  if (shape <= 0 || rate <= 0) return(1e10)   # keep the search in the valid region
  -sum(dgamma(x, shape = shape, rate = rate, log = TRUE))
}

# Method-of-moments starting values (a sensible initial guess matters)
m <- mean(x); v <- var(x)
start <- c(shape = m^2 / v, rate = m / v)

fit <- optim(par = start, fn = nll, hessian = TRUE)

fit$par          # the MLEs (shape, rate)
```


   shape     rate 
2.606774 1.691830 


optim returns the fitted parameters in fit$par, and because we asked for hessian = TRUE it also returns the curvature of the negative log-likelihood at the optimum — which is the observed information matrix \(J(\hat\theta)\). Inverting it gives the variance–covariance matrix, whose diagonal square-roots are the standard errors:


Code
```{r}
# Observed information = Hessian of the NEGATIVE log-likelihood
J  <- fit$hessian
V  <- solve(J)               # variance-covariance matrix
se <- sqrt(diag(V))          # standard errors for (shape, rate)

# Wald 95% CIs for each parameter
estimate <- fit$par
ci <- cbind(estimate,
            lower = estimate - 1.96 * se,
            upper = estimate + 1.96 * se)
round(ci, 3)
```


      estimate lower upper
shape    2.607 2.213 3.000
rate     1.692 1.410 1.973


Both intervals comfortably contain the true values (shape \(2.5\), rate \(1.5\)). A few practical notes that apply to almost any optim problem:






TipGetting optim to behave




Always work with the negative log-likelihood — optim minimises by default.
Guard the valid region. Returning a huge value (1e10) when a parameter strays out of bounds stops the optimiser wandering into NaNs. For box constraints you can instead use method = "L-BFGS-B" with lower=/upper=.
Choose sensible starting values. Method-of-moments estimates (as above) are a reliable starting point; a poor start can land the optimiser in a flat region or a local optimum.
Use hessian = TRUE whenever you want standard errors — it saves you differentiating the log-likelihood by hand.
The off-diagonal of V is the covariance between the parameter estimates: here shape and rate are strongly correlated, which is typical and is exactly the kind of thing a one-parameter analysis would miss.

title: Simulation in R: Tractable and Intractable Problems
section: When even the Hessian is not enough
text:
When even the Hessian is not enough
The Hessian-based standard errors above are themselves an asymptotic approximation — they assume the same normality from the previous page, now in two dimensions. If the sample is small or the likelihood is skewed, you can drop the formula entirely and bootstrap the whole two-parameter fit, re-running optim on each resampled data set:


Code
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

B <- 1000
bootPar <- matrix(NA, nrow = B, ncol = 2,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, c("shape", "rate")))
for (b in 1:B) {
  xStar <- sample(x, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  nllStar <- function(theta) {
    if (any(theta <= 0)) return(1e10)
    -sum(dgamma(xStar, shape = theta[1], rate = theta[2], log = TRUE))
  }
  bootPar[b, ] <- optim(par = fit$par, fn = nllStar)$par
}

# Bootstrap SEs and CIs, no Hessian required
rbind(
  bootstrapSe = apply(bootPar, 2, sd),
  ciLower     = apply(bootPar, 2, quantile, 0.025),
  ciUpper     = apply(bootPar, 2, quantile, 0.975)
) |> round(3)
```


            shape  rate
bootstrapSe 0.199 0.139
ciLower     2.293 1.480
ciUpper     3.078 2.018


The bootstrap standard errors closely track the Hessian-based ones — the same cross-check we did in the one-parameter case, now confirming that the asymptotic two-parameter fit is trustworthy here.

title: Introduction to Statistics
text:
“To call in the statistician after the experiment is done may be no more than asking him to perform a post-mortem examination: he may be able to say what the experiment died of.” — R. A. Fisher
This section introduces parametric statistical inference from the frequentist point of view. Before we develop any machinery, it is worth being very clear about what statistics actually is, and how it differs from the closely related — but logically opposite — subject of probability.

title: Introduction to Statistics
text:
Why use the frequentist approach?

No prior required. You do not have to invent or justify a prior distribution, which can feel arbitrary and can be hard to defend to a sceptical audience.
Objectivity and reproducibility. Two analysts with the same data and the same model get the same answer; there is no subjective input to argue about.
Well-understood guarantees. Confidence intervals and p-values come with clean long-run frequency properties, and many estimators have known optimality results.
Computational simplicity. Maximum likelihood estimates are often available in closed form or via fast optimisation, with no need for the heavy sampling machinery Bayesian methods sometimes require.
It is the lingua franca. Most introductory courses, regulatory frameworks, and scientific journals are built around frequentist tools, so fluency in them is essential.

title: Introduction to Statistics
section: Why someone might prefer Bayesian instead
text:
Why someone might prefer Bayesian instead
For balance: Bayesian methods let you incorporate genuine prior knowledge, give intuitively interpretable probability statements about \(\theta\), handle small samples and complex hierarchical models gracefully, and update naturally as new data arrives. The “right” choice depends on the problem — but this section is firmly frequentist, and that choice shapes every method that follows.

title: Introduction to Statistics
text:
Method of moments (MoM)
This is the older and more elementary idea. Every distribution’s theoretical moments — its mean, variance, and so on — are functions of the unknown parameter \(\theta\). For example, a Poisson(\(\lambda\)) has mean \(\lambda\); an Exponential(\(\lambda\)) has mean \(1/\lambda\); a Normal has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).






NoteIn a nutshell: what is a ‘moment’?



A moment is just an average of a power of the data — nothing more exotic than that. The 1st moment is the average of the values themselves, i.e. the mean. The 2nd moment is the average of the squared values, and once you centre it you get the variance. So whenever you read “match the moments,” read “match the averages.”


The method of moments simply says: compute the same moments from the data and set them equal to the theoretical ones, then solve for \(\theta\). If the model’s mean is \(1/\lambda\) and the sample mean is \(\bar x\), we set \(1/\lambda = \bar x\) and read off \(\hat\lambda = 1/\bar x\). With \(p\) unknown parameters we match the first \(p\) moments to get \(p\) equations.
Why it is useful: it is fast, requires no calculus, and almost always gives a tidy closed-form answer. That makes it an excellent source of starting values for the numerical optimisers we meet later (you will see exactly this on the Simulation page, where method-of-moments estimates seed a Gamma fit). Its weakness: it ignores the full shape of the distribution — it only looks at a few summary moments — so it is generally less efficient (noisier) than the next method.

title: Introduction to Statistics
text:
Maximum likelihood (MLE)
The second recipe asks a more demanding question: of all the candidate values of \(\theta\), which one makes the data we actually observed most probable? That value is the maximum likelihood estimate. Rather than matching a couple of moments, it uses the entire probability model and every data point at once.
This extra effort is rewarded. As later pages show, the MLE comes with strong guarantees — it converges to the truth as data accumulates, it is asymptotically the most precise estimator possible, and its uncertainty falls straight out of the curvature of the likelihood. These properties are why maximum likelihood, not the method of moments, is the backbone of this section.









Method of moments
Maximum likelihood




Core idea
Match sample moments to model moments
Maximise the probability of the observed data


Uses
A few summary moments
The whole distribution, every data point


Closed form?
Usually yes — quick algebra
Sometimes; often needs a numerical search


Efficiency
Lower (noisier estimates)
Highest possible (asymptotically)


Typical role
Quick estimate / starting values
The main workhorse of the section









TipGoing further 🚀



The two recipes usually land near each other, but they can flatly disagree. Try the Uniform\((0,\theta)\) model: the method of moments gives \(\hat\theta_{\text{MoM}} = 2\bar x\) (the mean of a Uniform\((0,\theta)\) is \(\theta/2\)), whereas the MLE is \(\hat\theta_{\text{MLE}} = \max_i x_i\) — the largest value seen. Simulate it and see for yourself:


Code
```{r}
set.seed(1)
x <- runif(50, min = 0, max = 10)   # true theta = 10
c(MoM = 2 * mean(x), MLE = max(x))
```


      MoM       MLE 
10.651857  9.919061 


The MoM can even produce an estimate below the largest observation — an “impossible” value the data has already ruled out. Which estimator would you trust here, and why?








NoteThe plan



We will use maximum likelihood as our primary tool because of its optimality, and keep method of moments in our back pocket for quick estimates and for seeding numerical optimisers. The next page builds the maximum-likelihood machinery from the ground up.

title: Asymptotics and Confidence Intervals
text:
The previous page ended with a powerful claim: for large samples, the MLE is approximately normal, \[
\hat{\theta} \;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\theta,\; \tfrac{1}{I(\theta)}\right).
\] That single result is what lets us turn a point estimate into a confidence interval. But notice the words “approximately” and “for large samples” — this is asymptotic theory, holding only in the limit as the sample size grows. This page explains the asymptotic results and uses them to construct confidence intervals. The next page shows what to do when these formulas run out and we must turn to simulation instead.
flowchart LR
  MLE["MLE θ̂"] --> AN["Asymptotic normality<br/>θ̂ ≈ N(θ, 1/I(θ))"]
  AN --> W["Wald interval<br/>θ̂ ± 1.96·se"]
  AN --> LR["Likelihood-ratio interval<br/>invert 2[ℓ(θ̂) − ℓ(θ)]"]

title: Asymptotics and Confidence Intervals
text:
Consistency
The MLE converges to the truth as data accumulates: \[
\hat{\theta} \xrightarrow{\;p\;} \theta \qquad \text{as } n \to \infty.
\] With enough data, the estimate lands on the true value. This is the bare-minimum guarantee we want from any estimator.






NoteIn a nutshell: the two arrows



These pages use two kinds of limit arrow. \(\xrightarrow{\;p\;}\) (“converges in probability”) means the estimate gets arbitrarily close to a fixed number as \(n\) grows — here, the truth \(\theta\). \(\xrightarrow{\;d\;}\) (“converges in distribution”) is weaker: the quantity stays random, but its whole distribution settles into a fixed shape — below, a normal. Roughly: \(\xrightarrow{p}\) pins down a value, \(\xrightarrow{d}\) pins down a distribution.

title: Asymptotics and Confidence Intervals
text:
Asymptotic normality
Suitably scaled, the estimation error is normally distributed in the limit: \[
\sqrt{n}\,(\hat{\theta} - \theta) \xrightarrow{\;d\;} \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\; \tfrac{1}{i(\theta)}\right),
\] where \(i(\theta)\) is the Fisher information from a single observation and \(I(\theta) = n\,i(\theta)\) is the total. Rearranged for practical use: \[
\hat{\theta} \;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\theta,\; \tfrac{1}{I(\theta)}\right).
\]






NoteIn a nutshell: little i vs big I



Watch the case carefully — they are different quantities. Lowercase \(i(\theta)\) is the information from one observation; uppercase \(I(\theta) = n\,i(\theta)\) is the information from all \(n\) observations stacked together. The lowercase version appears here because the \(\sqrt{n}\) scaling pulls out the per-observation amount; everywhere else in this section we use the total, big \(I\).








NoteWhere the normal comes from



This is the Central Limit Theorem in disguise. The score is a sum of independent contributions, one per observation, so it is asymptotically normal — and the MLE inherits that normality. This is why the normal distribution appears everywhere in frequentist inference, even when the data itself is not normal.

title: Asymptotics and Confidence Intervals
text:
Efficiency
Among all reasonable (asymptotically unbiased) estimators, the MLE achieves the smallest possible variance in the limit — the Cramér–Rao lower bound, \(1/I(\theta)\). You cannot do better asymptotically, which is the deep reason maximum likelihood is the default tool.






NoteIn a nutshell: the Cramér–Rao lower bound



The Cramér–Rao lower bound is a speed limit on precision: no unbiased estimator can have a variance below \(1/I(\theta)\), no matter how clever it is. What makes the MLE special is that it reaches this floor asymptotically — it is as precise as any unbiased estimator is allowed to be.








WarningAsymptotic means approximate



These results hold as \(n\to\infty\). In a small sample they may be poor: a Wald interval can stray outside a parameter’s natural range (e.g. a probability below 0) or have the wrong coverage. When \(n\) is small or the model is awkward, the simulation methods on the next page are often more trustworthy — and they let you check whether the asymptotics can be trusted at all.

title: Asymptotics and Confidence Intervals
text:
The Wald interval
This is the direct consequence of asymptotic normality. Using the standard error \(\operatorname{se}(\hat{\theta}) = 1/\sqrt{I(\hat{\theta})}\): \[
\boxed{\,\hat{\theta} \;\pm\; z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\operatorname{se}(\hat{\theta})\,}
\qquad
\hat{\theta} \pm 1.96\,\operatorname{se}(\hat{\theta}) \text{ for } 95\%.
\]
Pros: trivial to compute — just an estimate and its standard error. Cons: it assumes the log-likelihood is symmetric (parabolic) around the peak, which fails for skewed likelihoods and small samples.

title: Asymptotics and Confidence Intervals
text:
The likelihood-ratio interval
A more accurate interval uses the shape of the log-likelihood directly rather than assuming it is a parabola. The likelihood-ratio statistic \[
W(\theta) = 2\big[\,\ell(\hat{\theta}) - \ell(\theta)\,\big]
\] is asymptotically \(\chi^2_1\). Inverting it gives the interval of all \(\theta\) not rejected at level \(\alpha\): \[
\boxed{\,\big\{\,\theta : 2[\ell(\hat{\theta}) - \ell(\theta)] \le \chi^2_{1,\,1-\alpha}\,\big\}\,}
\] where \(\chi^2_{1,\,0.95} \approx 3.84\). This interval respects the likelihood’s true (possibly asymmetric) shape and stays within the parameter’s natural range, so it is generally preferred when it is feasible to compute.

Why a chi-squared, and why “invert” it?
Two questions deserve a proper answer: why does the \(\chi^2\) distribution appear at all, and what does “inverting” the statistic mean?
Why \(\chi^2_1\) — Wilks’ theorem. Expand the log-likelihood with a Taylor series around its peak \(\hat\theta\). The first-derivative term vanishes (the score is zero at the MLE), so the leading term is quadratic: \[
\ell(\theta) \approx \ell(\hat\theta) - \tfrac{1}{2}\,I(\hat\theta)\,(\theta - \hat\theta)^2.
\] Substituting this into the likelihood-ratio statistic gives \[
W(\theta) = 2\big[\ell(\hat\theta) - \ell(\theta)\big] \approx I(\hat\theta)\,(\hat\theta - \theta)^2 = \left(\frac{\hat\theta - \theta}{\operatorname{se}(\hat\theta)}\right)^2.
\] The bracket on the right is, by asymptotic normality, a standard normal \(Z\). And a squared standard normal is by definition a chi-squared with one degree of freedom: \(Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1\). That is the whole reason the \(\chi^2_1\) appears — it is the squared version of the same normal that powered the Wald interval. (This result, that \(2[\ell(\hat\theta)-\ell(\theta)] \to \chi^2_1\), is Wilks’ theorem; the single degree of freedom counts the one parameter being constrained.)






NoteWald and likelihood-ratio are the same thing, to first order



The Taylor expansion above shows the Wald and likelihood-ratio intervals agree exactly when the log-likelihood is truly parabolic. They differ only by the higher-order terms the expansion drops — which is precisely the asymmetry of the real likelihood. So the LR interval is “the Wald idea, but using the genuine curve instead of its parabolic approximation.” This is why they nearly coincide at large \(n\) but the LR interval is more faithful when the likelihood is skewed.


Why “invert”. A hypothesis test fixes a candidate value \(\theta_0\) and asks “is the data compatible with it?” — we reject \(\theta_0\) when \(W(\theta_0) > \chi^2_{1,\,0.95} \approx 3.84\). A confidence interval turns this around: it is the set of all candidate values we would not reject. Inverting the test means sweeping \(\theta_0\) across its whole range and collecting every value that survives: \[
\text{CI} = \{\theta : W(\theta) \le 3.84\}.
\] The duality “confidence interval = the values a test does not reject” is general and powerful — it is exactly what the worked example below does numerically, scanning a grid of \(\theta\) and keeping those under the cut-off.





flowchart LR
  W["Wald CI<br/>θ̂ ± 1.96·se"] --> W2["Fast, simple<br/>assumes a symmetric<br/>(parabolic) likelihood"]
  L["Likelihood-ratio CI<br/>invert 2[ℓ(θ̂) − ℓ(θ)]"] --> L2["Uses the true likelihood shape<br/>respects parameter ranges<br/>more accurate in small samples"]

A basic summary table
To create a summary table, we could manually calculate every entry and then create a dataset of these values and then create the table. However, it is much quicker (and easier) to use the summarise() function that comes with the dplyr package.






Note



The dplyr package will be installed/active if you have tidyverse. Alternatively, you can directly install and activate the package with the following commands:


Code
```{r}
#| warning: false # will remove output messages

###| Package downloading and activating
# install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)
```


If you are using RStudio, you can check which packages are installed using the bottom right window.


The following code gives some examples of how to extract various summary statistics using the summarise() command.


Code
```{r}
###| Basic summary table on continuous data
cars %>%
  summarise("Num. observations" = n(),
            "Mean mpg" = mean(mpg),
            "Range displacement" = max(disp)-min(disp),
            "Median horsepower" = median(hp))
```

Things get more complicated for categorical factors. We may need to use the length(), which() and unique() functions to find our desired statistics.






NoteIn a nutshell: counting TRUEs



length(which(vs == 1)) counts the rows where the condition vs == 1 is TRUE. A simpler equivalent is sum(vs == 1), because R treats each TRUE as 1 and each FALSE as 0 when summing.




Code
```{r}
###| Basic summary table on categorical data

  summarise("vs 1" = length(which(vs == 1)),

            "Num. manufacturers" = length(unique(manufacturer))
  )
```

title: Univariate Data
text:
A sensible starting point for any data analysis is to look at each important variable on its own. Univariate graphs do exactly this: they show the distribution of a single variable at a time. That variable might be categorical (for example diet, taxonomic order, or conservation status) or quantitative (such as sleep duration, body weight, or brain weight).
Throughout this chapter we use the msleep dataset, which contains sleep times and weights for 83 different mammals. We focus on three variables: the diet (vore) and taxonomic order (order) of the animals, and the total amount of sleep they get (sleep_total).

title: Univariate Data
text:
Categorical variables
Both the diet of the mammals and their taxonomic order are categorical variables. The distribution of a single categorical variable is most commonly shown using a bar chart. Other options include pie charts, and—less frequently—tree maps or waffle charts.

Bar charts
Below, we plot a simple bar chart to display the distribution of mammals by diet (vore).


Code
library(ggplot2)
data(msleep, package = "ggplot2")

# plot the distribution of diet (vore)
# We filter out NAs for a cleaner plot
library(dplyr)
mclean <- msleep %>% filter(!is.na(vore))

ggplot(mclean, aes(x = vore)) +
  geom_bar()









From this plot we can immediately see that most mammals in this dataset are herbivores, followed closely by omnivores and carnivores, with insectivores being the smallest group.


Percentages
Instead of showing raw counts, bars can also represent percentages. In a bar chart, aes(x = vore) is shorthand for aes(x = vore, y = after_stat(count)), where count is the frequency in each category. By working with this quantity explicitly, we can convert counts into percentages.






NoteIn a nutshell: what after_stat means



after_stat() tells ggplot2 to compute the bar heights itself from the data (here, by counting how many mammals fall in each category), rather than you supplying a y value directly.




Code
```{r}
# plot the distribution as percentages
ggplot(mclean,
       aes(x = vore, y = after_stat(count/sum(count)))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Diet",
       y = "Percent",
       title  = "Mammals by diet") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
```









Here, the scales package is used to format the y-axis labels as percentages.



Sorting categories
It is often helpful to order categories by their frequency. To do this, we first calculate the counts explicitly and then reorder the categories using reorder(). Setting stat = "identity" tells ggplot2 not to compute counts internally.


Code
```{r}
# calculate number of mammals in each diet category
pdat <- mclean %>%
  count(vore)
```


The resulting dataset is shown below:



vore
n




carni
19


herbi
32


insecti
5


omni
20



We can now use this dataset to create a sorted bar chart.


Code
```{r}
# plot the bars in ascending order
ggplot(pdat,
       aes(x = reorder(vore, n), y = n)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity") +
  labs(x = "Diet",
       y = "Frequency",
       title  = "Mammals by diet")
```









The bars are ordered from smallest to largest frequency. Using reorder(vore, -n) would reverse this order.



Labelling bars
Sometimes it is useful to display the numerical values directly on the bars.


Code
```{r}
# plot the bars with numeric labels
ggplot(pdat,
       aes(x = vore, y = n)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust=-0.5) +
  labs(x = "Diet",
       y = "Frequency",
       title  = "Mammals by diet")
```









Here, geom_text() adds the labels, and vjust controls their vertical positioning.
Putting these ideas together, we can create a bar chart showing percentages, ordered from most to least frequent, and labelled accordingly.


Code
library(scales)
pdat <- mclean %>%
  count(vore) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         pctlabel = paste0(round(pct*100), "%"))

# plot the bars as percentages,
# in descending order with bar labels
ggplot(pdat,
       aes(x = reorder(vore, -pct), y = pct)) +
  geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="indianred3", color="black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = pctlabel), vjust=-0.25) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = "Diet",
       y = "Percent",
       title  = "Mammals by diet")












Overlapping labels
When there are many categories or when labels are long, axis labels can overlap. This is clear when plotting the taxonomic order of the mammals.


Code
```{r}
# basic bar chart with overlapping labels
ggplot(msleep, aes(x=order)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Taxonomic Order",
       y = "Frequency",
       title = "Mammals by Order")
```









One solution is to flip the axes.


Code
```{r}
# horizontal bar chart
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = order)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "Frequency",
       title = "Mammals by Order") +
  coord_flip()
```









Alternatively, labels can be rotated.


Code
```{r}
# bar chart with rotated labels
ggplot(msleep, aes(x=order)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "Frequency",
       title = "Mammals by Order") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```









A third option is to stagger the labels by inserting line breaks.


Code
```{r}
# bar chart with staggered labels
lbls <- paste0(c("","\n"), unique(msleep$order))
# Note: In real usage, ensure labels match factor levels order
ggplot(msleep,
       aes(x=factor(order, labels = lbls))) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "",
       y = "Frequency",
       title = "Mammals by Order")
```









In practice, it is usually best to avoid rotated labels where possible, as they are harder to read and increase cognitive load for the reader.




Pie charts
Pie charts are often debated in statistics. For comparing category frequencies, bar charts are generally superior because humans judge lengths more accurately than areas. However, if the goal is to show how each category relates to the whole, and there are only a few categories, pie charts can still be useful.
A pie chart in ggplot2 is essentially a bar chart plotted on a polar coordinate system.


Code
```{r}
# Prepare data for pie chart
pdat <- mclean %>%
  count(vore) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  mutate(label = scales::percent(prop))

# Create pie chart
ggplot(pdat, aes(x = "", y = prop, fill = vore)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Mammals by diet")
```









We use coord_polar("y") to transform the bar chart into a circle. theme_void() is used to remove the background, axis grid, and labels that are not necessary for a pie chart.
To place labels inside the slices, we can use geom_text() with position_stack().


Code
```{r}
# Create pie chart with labels
ggplot(pdat, aes(x = "", y = prop, fill = vore)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            color = "white",
            size = 4) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Mammals by diet") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```









This plot makes it clear, for example, that roughly 42% of the mammals in this dataset are herbivores.



Tree maps
Tree maps provide another alternative to pie charts and are particularly useful when there are many categories, such as the taxonomic orders in our dataset.


Code
library(treemapify)

# create a treemap of mammal orders
pdat <- msleep %>%
  count(order)

ggplot(pdat,
       aes(fill = order, area = n)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  labs(title = "Mammals by Order")









Adding labels makes the plot more informative.


Code
```{r}
# create a treemap with tile labels
ggplot(pdat,
       aes(fill = order, area = n, label = order)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_text(colour = "white", place = "centre") +
  labs(title = "Mammals by Order") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```












Waffle charts
A waffle chart (also called a grid plot or square pie chart) represents proportions using a grid of squares. While dedicated packages exist, we can create a waffle chart in standard ggplot2 by treating the data as a grid of tiles (dedicated packages sometimes get removed so it’s better to have a more sustainable way to make graphs that don’t rely on external packages).
We begin by sorting the data and assigning logical x and y coordinates to each mammal to create a 10-column grid.


Code
```{r}
# Prepare data: Sort by diet to cluster colors
waffle <- mclean %>%
  arrange(vore) %>%
  mutate(
    # Create x and y coordinates for a 10-column grid
    x = (row_number() - 1) %% 10,
    y = (row_number() - 1) %/% 10
  )

# Create the chart using geom_tile
ggplot(waffle, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = vore)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +  # white borders create the "grid" look
  coord_fixed() +               # ensures squares remain square
  theme_void() +                # removes axes and backgrounds
  labs(title = "Mammals by Diet",
       caption = "1 square = 1 mammal")
```









This chart displays every individual mammal as a single square, making it easy to visualise the sample size alongside the proportions.

title: Univariate Data
text:
Quantitative variables
In the msleep dataset, sleep_total (total sleep in hours) is a quantitative variable. Common ways to visualise the distribution of a single quantitative variable include histograms, kernel density plots, and dot plots.

Histograms
Histograms are the most widely used tool for visualising quantitative data. The range of values is divided into adjacent bins of equal width, and the number of observations in each bin is shown as a bar.


Code
library(ggplot2)

# plot the sleep distribution using a histogram
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Mammal sleep distribution",
       x = "Total Sleep (hours)")









The distribution appears somewhat bimodal, with many mammals sleeping around 10 hours, but a significant number sleeping much less or much more.


Bins and bandwidths
The choice of the number of bins (or equivalently the bin width) has a large impact on the appearance of a histogram. The default is 30 bins, but it is often useful to experiment.


Code
```{r}
# plot the histogram with 15 bins
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "cornflowerblue",
                 color = "white",
                 bins = 15) +
  labs(title="Mammal sleep distribution",
       subtitle = "number of bins = 15",
       x = "Total Sleep (hours)")
```









Alternatively, you can specify the bin width directly.


Code
```{r}
# plot the histogram with a binwidth of 2 hours
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "cornflowerblue",
                 color = "white",
                 binwidth = 2) +
  labs(title="Mammal sleep distribution",
       subtitle = "binwidth = 2 hours",
       x = "Total Sleep (hours)")
```









As before, the y-axis can show counts or percentages.


Code
```{r}
library(scales)
ggplot(msleep,
       aes(x = sleep_total, y= after_stat(count/sum(count)))) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "cornflowerblue",
                 color = "white",
                 binwidth = 2) +
  labs(title="Mammal sleep distribution",
       y = "Percent",
       x = "Total Sleep (hours)") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent)
```













Kernel density plots
A kernel density plot provides a smooth alternative to a histogram. The idea is to estimate the underlying probability density function of a continuous variable, producing a smooth curve whose total area equals one.


Code
```{r}
# Create a kernel density plot of sleep
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total)) +
  geom_density() +
  labs(title = "Mammal sleep distribution")
```









The area under the curve between two time points represents the proportion of mammals in that sleep range.


Code
```{r}
# Create a kernel density plot of sleep
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total)) +
  geom_density(fill = "indianred3") +
  labs(title = "Mammal sleep distribution")
```











Smoothing parameter
The amount of smoothing is controlled by the bandwidth parameter bw. Larger values produce smoother curves, while smaller values reveal more detail.


Code
```{r}
# default bandwidth for the sleep variable
bw.nrd0(msleep$sleep_total)
```


[1] 1.637473




Code
```{r}
# Create a kernel density plot of sleep
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total)) +
  geom_density(fill = "deepskyblue",
               bw = 1) +
  labs(title = "Mammal sleep distribution",
       subtitle = "bandwidth = 1")
```









Kernel density plots are useful for identifying where observations are concentrated, although the interpretation of the y-axis can be less intuitive for non-statisticians, so do keep this in mind.




Dot plots
A dot plot is another alternative to the histogram. The data are grouped into bins, but each individual observation is shown as a dot. This approach works best for relatively small datasets like msleep.


Code
# plot the sleep distribution using a dotplot
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total)) +
  geom_dotplot() +
  labs(title = "Mammal sleep distribution",
       y = "Proportion",
       x = "Total Sleep (hours)")









Many additional options are available; see ?geom_dotplot for further details.
These are just a couple of ways you could visualise one variable, do explore to find more!






TipGoing further 🚀



Two modern packages give you slicker distribution displays. ggbeeswarm spreads overlapping points sideways so none are hidden, and ggridges draws a density curve per group, stacked into a ridgeline plot.


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ggbeeswarm)
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = vore, y = sleep_total)) +
  geom_beeswarm()

library(ggridges)
ggplot(msleep, aes(x = sleep_total, y = vore)) +
  geom_density_ridges()
```

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
This chapter covers specialised visualisation techniques that don’t fit neatly into other categories but are incredibly useful for specific types of data and questions. Think of these as tools for your “advanced visualisation toolkit”—you won’t use them every day, but when you need them, they’re perfect for the job.
We’ll explore: - Visualising three-dimensional relationships - Displaying flows and transitions - Creating comparison matrices - Specialised chart types for specific purposes
Let’s load our packages:


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
Basic Bubble Chart
Let’s explore the relationship between penguin flipper length, body mass, and bill length:


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, 
                     y = body_mass_g,
                     size = bill_length_mm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Penguin Physical Characteristics",
       x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y = "Body Mass (g)",
       size = "Bill Length (mm)")

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
Enhanced Bubble Chart
Let’s improve this with better styling and add a fourth variable (species) using colour:


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm,
                     y = body_mass_g,
                     size = bill_length_mm,
                     color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, shape = 16) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 12)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Four Variables in One Visualization",
       subtitle = "Bubble size represents bill length",
       x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y = "Body Mass (g)",
       size = "Bill Length (mm)",
       color = "Species") +
  theme_minimal()









The scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 12)) controls the minimum and maximum bubble sizes.






Note



Bubble charts are controversial because humans are better at judging length than area. Use them when the approximate relationship is more important than exact values.

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
Creating a Correlation Matrix
Let’s visualise correlations between penguin measurements:


Code
# Prepare data - select numeric columns only
pnum <- penguins %>%
  select(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, 
         flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) %>%
  na.omit()

# Calculate correlation matrix
corMat <- cor(pnum)

# Convert to long format for ggplot
library(tidyr)
corLong <- corMat %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(var1 = rownames(.)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -var1, 
               names_to = "var2", 
               values_to = "correlation")

# Create heatmap
ggplot(corLong, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2)), 
            color = "black", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation Matrix of Penguin Measurements",
       x = "", y = "", fill = "Correlation") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))









Strong positive correlations appear in red, negative correlations in blue, and weak correlations in white.

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
Custom Scatterplot Matrix
You can customise the appearance with your own functions:


Code
# Custom function for density plots
myDensity <- function(data, mapping, ...) {
  ggplot(data = data, mapping = mapping) + 
    geom_density(alpha = 0.6, fill = "steelblue")
}

# Custom function for scatterplots
myScatter <- function(data, mapping, ...) {
  ggplot(data = data, mapping = mapping) + 
    geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) + 
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "darkred", linewidth = 0.8)
}

# Create customized matrix
pnumOnly <- penguins %>%
  select(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, 
         flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) %>%
  na.omit()

ggpairs(pnumOnly,
        lower = list(continuous = myScatter),
        diag = list(continuous = myDensity)) +
  labs(title = "Penguin Measurements: Detailed Relationships") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
Basic Alluvial Diagram
Let’s examine how penguins are distributed across species, islands, and sex:


Code
library(ggalluvial)

# Prepare data
flows <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(sex)) %>%
  group_by(species, island, sex) %>%
  summarise(count = n(), .groups = "drop")

# Create alluvial diagram
ggplot(flows,
       aes(axis1 = species,
           axis2 = island,
           axis3 = sex,
           y = count)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = species), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_stratum(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", aes(label = after_stat(stratum))) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Species", "Island", "Sex"),
                   expand = c(0.1, 0.1)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Penguin Distribution Across Categories",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









How to read this:

Start on the left with species
Follow the flows to see how each species is distributed across islands
Continue following to see the sex distribution
Flow width represents the number of penguins

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
Enhanced Alluvial Diagram
Let’s create a more detailed version with better styling:


Code
ggplot(flows,
       aes(axis1 = species,
           axis2 = island,
           axis3 = sex,
           y = count)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(fill = species), 
                color = "black", 
                alpha = 0.8,
                curve_type = "sigmoid") +
  geom_stratum(alpha = 0.9, color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(stat = "stratum", 
            aes(label = after_stat(stratum)),
            size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Species", "Island", "Sex"),
                   expand = c(0.15, 0.15)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "How Penguins are Distributed",
       subtitle = "Following the flow from species through island to sex",
       y = "Number of Penguins",
       fill = "Species") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"))

title: Specialised Visualisation Techniques
text:
Waterfall Chart with Net Total
Let’s add a total column to show the final balance:


Code
waterfall(budget,
          calc_total = TRUE,
          total_axis_text = "Remaining",
          total_rect_text_color = "black",
          total_rect_color = "gold") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(title = "Research Project Financial Flow",
       subtitle = "Tracking income and expenses",
       x = "", y = "") +
  theme_minimal()









This shows clearly how the initial grant is allocated across different expenses.

title: Introduction to Data Visualisation
text:
“The greatest value of a picture is when it forces us to notice what we never expected to see.” - John W. Tukey

The subsections here will cover a few data visualisation techniques using ggplot2. The ggplot library is extremely powerful for data visualisation for a number of reasons: it is trivial to add and remove features from graphs, it is one of a few R libraries that are always being worked on and updated, and many more reasons we will discover here.
This section is built to help you choose the right graph for the right question. The same data can be shown in many ways; the goal is to make your message clear.

Why this section matters
Visualisation is not just decoration. Good graphs allow you to:

spot patterns and trends,
compare groups or changes over time,
communicate results to others,
check whether a model is sensible.



When to use base R vs ggplot2

Use base R for quick exploratory plots and simple visuals.
Use ggplot2 when you need more control over labels, colours, layouts, or multi-layer graphics.

This section covers:


a review on data importing
how baseR and ggplot plot graphs,
how to approach univariate data,
how to approach bivariate data,
how to approach time-dependent data,
how to approach multivariate data,
miscellaneous graphs,
how to customise graphs,
general advice on data visualisation

title: Graph Customisation
text:
When you first create plots in R, the default settings work well for exploring your data. However, when you’re preparing visualisations for presentations, reports, or publications, you’ll want to polish them to make your message clearer and more visually appealing.
In this tutorial, we’ll learn how to customise various aspects of ggplot2 graphs including axes, colours, labels, legends, and themes. We’ll primarily use the palmerpenguins dataset, which contains measurements of three penguin species from islands in Antarctica.
First, let’s load our packages and data:


Code
library(ggplot2)


Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3


Code
library(palmerpenguins)


Warning: package 'palmerpenguins' was built under R version 4.4.3


Code
library(dplyr)

title: Graph Customisation
text:
Numeric Axes
You can control numeric axes using scale_x_continuous() and scale_y_continuous(). The most useful options are:

breaks: Where to place tick marks and labels
limits: The minimum and maximum values to display



Code
# Basic plot
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(30, 60, by = 5),
                     limits = c(30, 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(13, 22, by = 2),
                     limits = c(13, 22)) +
  labs(title = "Penguin Bill Dimensions",
       x = "Bill Length (mm)",
       y = "Bill Depth (mm)")















Tip



The seq() function creates a sequence of numbers. For example, seq(30, 60, by = 5) creates: 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60.

title: Graph Customisation
text:
Formatting Numbers
The scales package provides helpful functions for formatting axis labels:

comma: Adds commas to large numbers (1000 becomes 1,000)
dollar: Adds currency symbols
percent: Converts decimals to percentages

In the code chunk below, we create a random dataset by sampling from normal and uniform distributions for demonstrative purposes. Don’t worry, the penguins will come back in the next example!


Code
```{r}
# Create sample data
set.seed(42)
pop <- data.frame(
  city = paste("City", 1:40),
  population = rnorm(40, 250000, 80000),
  employment_rate = runif(40, 0.55, 0.85),
  median_income = rnorm(40, 65000, 15000)
)

ggplot(pop, aes(x = population, y = employment_rate)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Population vs Employment Rate",
       x = "City Population",
       y = "Employment Rate")
```

title: Graph Customisation
text:
Categorical Axes
For categorical variables, use scale_x_discrete() or scale_y_discrete(). Returning to our penguins dataset:


Code
```{r}
# Apply categorical variable scaling
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "coral") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Adélie\nPenguin", 
                              "Chinstrap\nPenguin", 
                              "Gentoo\nPenguin")) +
  labs(title = "Number of Penguins by Species",
       x = "Species",
       y = "Count")
```















Note



\n creates a line break in text labels.

title: Graph Customisation
text:
Date Axes
Working with dates requires scale_x_date() or scale_y_date(). We use the economics dataset for this:


Code
```{r}
# Using the economics dataset
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy / 1000)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkblue", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "10 years",
               date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(title = "US Unemployment Over Time",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Unemployed (thousands)")
```















Note



We use date_ for breaks and labels for dates.


Common date format codes:



Code
Meaning
Example




%d
Day of month
01-31


%m
Month number
01-12


%b
Abbreviated month
Jan


%B
Full month
January


%y
2-digit year
24


%Y
4-digit year
2024

title: Graph Customisation
text:
Setting Colours Manually
Use color for points and lines, and fill for bars and areas:


Code
# Single color
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Penguin Bill Measurements")









To assign specific colours to categories, use scale_color_manual() or scale_fill_manual():


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Adelie" = "darkorange",
                                "Chinstrap" = "purple",
                                "Gentoo" = "cyan4")) +
  labs(title = "Penguin Species Count",
       x = "Species",
       y = "Count",
       fill = "Species")

title: Graph Customisation
text:
Using Colour Palettes
Pre-designed colour palettes might be a starting point to inspire the final aesthetic you choose for your graph.

ColorBrewer Palettes
ColorBrewer provides carefully designed colour schemes:


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = island)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Penguin Species by Island",
       x = "Species",
       y = "Count",
       fill = "Island")











Viridis Palettes
Viridis palettes are colourblind-friendly and print well in greyscale:


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = island)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Penguin Species by Island",
       x = "Species",
       y = "Count",
       fill = "Island")















Note



Use _c for continuous variables (numbers) and _d for discrete variables (categories).

title: Graph Customisation
text:
Point Shapes
Change point shapes with the shape parameter:


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
                     shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Bill Dimensions by Species",
       shape = "Species")









Shapes 21-25 allow both fill and border colours:


Code
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, 
                     fill = species)) +
