title: Python for R Users: Setup and Basics
text:
You have spent this course learning R. Python is the other great language of data science, and a well-rounded statistician is fluent in both. This short section is a bridge for R users: rather than teaching programming from scratch, it maps what you already know in R onto Python, then introduces the two libraries that power data work — NumPy and pandas — so that the Python code in the Machine Learning section becomes readable and runnable. It also feeds directly into modules like ST236 (Python for Data Analytic Tasks).






NoteIn a nutshell: this is translation, not a fresh start



You are not learning to program again — you already can. You are learning to say the same things in a new language. An R vector becomes a NumPy array; a data.frame becomes a pandas DataFrame; dplyr becomes pandas. Keep your R knowledge in mind and read each Python idea as “the Python version of the R thing I know.”



Getting Python running
To follow along on your own machine you need a Python installation with the scientific libraries. Two easy routes:

Google Colab (colab.research.google.com) — a free, browser-based notebook with NumPy and pandas already installed. Nothing to set up; ideal for experimenting.
A local install — the Anaconda (or Miniconda) distribution bundles Python with NumPy, pandas and the rest of the scientific stack in one download.

The pages of this section actually run their Python code through R’s reticulate package, which lets a single document execute both R and Python. If you want to reproduce that locally, install reticulate and point it at a Python with the libraries:


Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("reticulate")
library(reticulate)
py_install(c("numpy", "pandas"))   # install the libraries into reticulate's Python
```


Everything below this point is genuinely executed, so the output you see is what Python really returns.


The five things that will trip up an R user
Before any code, internalise the handful of differences that cause 90% of beginner mistakes coming from R:






ImportantFive Python surprises for R users




Indexing starts at 0, not 1. The first element of a list is x[0]. And slices are end-exclusive: x[0:2] gives elements 0 and 1, not 2.
Assignment is =, not <-. (<- is not valid Python.)
Indentation is part of the syntax. Python has no { }; a consistent indent (usually 4 spaces) defines a block. Get it wrong and the code errors.
Methods, not functions. Where R writes mean(x), Python often writes x.mean() — the function “belongs to” the object and is called with a dot.
The naming convention is snake_case (my_data), not the camelCase or dot.case common in R.





Assignment and printing
R returns and prints the last value automatically; in Python you usually call print() to see output.


Code
```{python}
x = 5
y = 10
print(x + y)
```


15


The same in R, for comparison:


Code
```{r}
x <- 5
y <- 10
x + y
```


[1] 15




Types
Python’s basic types mirror R’s: integers, floating-point numbers, strings and booleans. The type() function reports them (note Python’s booleans are capitalised, True/False).


Code
```{python}
print(type(7))          # int
print(type(7.5))        # float
print(type("stats"))    # str
print(type(True))       # bool
```


<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'str'>
<class 'bool'>




Lists: Python’s everyday container
A Python list is the closest everyday analogue of an R vector — an ordered collection — though it can hold mixed types like an R list. The crucial difference is 0-based, end-exclusive indexing.


Code
```{python}
my_list = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

print(my_list[0])      # first element  -> 10   (R would be my_list[1])
print(my_list[1:3])    # indices 1 and 2 -> [20, 30]   (end 3 excluded)
print(my_list[-1])     # last element   -> 50
print(len(my_list))    # length         -> 5

my_list.append(60)     # add to the end (a method!)
print(my_list)
```


10
[20, 30]
50
5
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]








NoteIn a nutshell: lists do not do maths



Beware: a plain Python list does not behave like an R vector under arithmetic. [1, 2, 3] * 2 gives [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3] (it repeats the list), not [2, 4, 6]. For element-wise maths you need a NumPy array — which is exactly why NumPy exists, and the subject of the next page.




Dictionaries: the named-list analogue
A dictionary stores key–value pairs, like an R named list. You look values up by their key.


Code
```{python}
prices = {"apple": 0.50, "banana": 0.30, "cherry": 0.80}

print(prices["apple"])        # look up by key -> 0.5
print(list(prices.keys()))    # the keys
print(list(prices.values()))  # the values
```


0.5
['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
[0.5, 0.3, 0.8]




Loops and conditionals
The logic is identical to R; only the syntax (a colon and indentation instead of braces) changes. Note range(n) counts 0, 1, …, n-1.


Code
```{python}
for i in range(4):        # 0, 1, 2, 3
    print(i)
```


0
1
2
3




Code
```{python}
score = 72

if score >= 70:
    grade = "First"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "2:1"
else:
    grade = "lower"

print(grade)
```


First


Python’s logical operators are the words and, or, not (where R uses &, |, !), and equality is ==.


Functions
Defined with def, a colon, and an indented body. The return statement hands back the result (just like R’s return(), but here it is the norm). Default arguments work as in R.


Code
```{python}
def power(x, p=2):        # p defaults to 2
    return x ** p          # ** is exponentiation (R's ^)

print(power(5))            # 25
print(power(2, 10))        # 1024
```


25
1024




Importing libraries
Where R attaches a package with library(), Python imports a module, conventionally giving it a short alias. You then reach its functions through that alias with a dot.


Code
```{python}
import numpy as np

print(np.sqrt(16))        # use numpy's sqrt via the alias 'np'  -> 4.0
```


4.0


This import … as … line will start almost every Python data script you write — import numpy as np and import pandas as pd are practically universal.






TipGoing further 🚀



A few idioms that make Python feel natural once you know R’s equivalents: list comprehensions ([x**2 for x in range(5)]) are Python’s compact answer to sapply/vapply; f-strings (f"grade: {grade}") are its paste0/sprintf; and help(np.sqrt) (or ? in a notebook) is its ?. Because this document runs through reticulate, you can even pass objects between the languages — an R data frame myData is visible in Python as r.myData, and a Python object result is visible in R as py$result.




Where this section is going


NumPy — arrays and vectorised computing: the analogue of R’s vectorised vectors and matrices, and the foundation of all numerical Python.
pandas — DataFrames for data wrangling: the analogue of data.frame/tibble and dplyr, for filtering, transforming and summarising tabular data.
R vs Python — a reference page of the key differences and gotchas, and guidance on when to reach for which language.


With these three, the Python half of the Machine Learning section stops being decorative and becomes code you can read, run and adapt.

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
If you have spent any time with R, you have spent time with data.frames and tibbles, and almost certainly with dplyr and tidyr for wrangling them. Python’s answer to all of this is a single library: pandas. The idea of this page is simple — almost everything you already know how to do in the tidyverse has a direct pandas counterpart. We will lean on that knowledge throughout, so think of this as a translation exercise rather than learning something from scratch.
One small but important habit to flag up front: Python uses snake_case for names (mean_speed), whereas in this course we tend to write R in camelCase (meanSpeed). Keep an eye on that as you read.

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
The DataFrame: pandas’ tibble






NoteIn a nutshell: the DataFrame is pandas’ data.frame, and pandas is dplyr + tidyr



A pandas DataFrame is a rectangular table of columns, exactly like an R data.frame or tibble. The pandas library provides the verbs to wrangle it — filtering, selecting, mutating, arranging, grouping and summarising — playing the combined role of dplyr and tidyr. By convention you import it as pd.


Let us build a small DataFrame inline. We will use a handful of cars, with a numeric speed column and a categorical brand column to group by.


Code
```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

cars = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Mini", "Golf", "Polo", "Civic", "Jazz", "Corolla"],
    "brand": ["BMW", "VW", "VW", "Honda", "Honda", "Toyota"],
    "speed": [110, 130, 105, 125, 100, 120],
    "doors": [3, 5, 5, 5, 5, 4],
})

cars
```


      name   brand  speed  doors
0     Mini     BMW    110      3
1     Golf      VW    130      5
2     Polo      VW    105      5
3    Civic   Honda    125      5
4     Jazz   Honda    100      5
5  Corolla  Toyota    120      4


For contrast, here is the same table built in base R. It should feel very familiar:


Code
```{r}
cars <- data.frame(
  name  = c("Mini", "Golf", "Polo", "Civic", "Jazz", "Corolla"),
  brand = c("BMW", "VW", "VW", "Honda", "Honda", "Toyota"),
  speed = c(110, 130, 105, 125, 100, 120),
  doors = c(3, 5, 5, 5, 5, 4)
)

cars
```


     name  brand speed doors
1    Mini    BMW   110     3
2    Golf     VW   130     5
3    Polo     VW   105     5
4   Civic  Honda   125     5
5    Jazz  Honda   100     5
6 Corolla Toyota   120     4


The two are conceptually identical: named columns of equal length, each with its own type.

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
Inspecting a DataFrame
Before wrangling, you usually want to look at the shape and structure of your data. In R you reach for head(), dim(), names(), str() and summary(). pandas has a near one-to-one set of tools.


Code
```{python}
cars.head()        # first few rows, like head() in R
```


    name  brand  speed  doors
0   Mini    BMW    110      3
1   Golf     VW    130      5
2   Polo     VW    105      5
3  Civic  Honda    125      5
4   Jazz  Honda    100      5




Code
```{python}
cars.shape         # (rows, columns) — like dim()
```


(6, 4)




Code
```{python}
cars.columns       # column names — like names()
```


Index(['name', 'brand', 'speed', 'doors'], dtype='str')




Code
```{python}
cars.dtypes        # type of each column — like sapply(df, class)
```


name       str
brand      str
speed    int64
doors    int64
dtype: object




Code
```{python}
cars.describe()    # numeric summary — like summary() on numeric columns
```


           speed    doors
count    6.00000  6.00000
mean   115.00000  4.50000
std     11.83216  0.83666
min    100.00000  3.00000
25%    106.25000  4.25000
50%    115.00000  5.00000
75%    123.75000  5.00000
max    130.00000  5.00000


Note that describe() by default only summarises the numeric columns (speed and doors), which is usually what you want.

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
Selecting columns and rows
This is the first place where Python’s conventions differ a little, so it is worth slowing down.
Columns. Selecting a single column with df['col'] returns a Series (a one-dimensional labelled vector, like a single R column). Selecting a list of columns with df[['a', 'b']] returns a DataFrame.


Code
```{python}
cars["speed"]              # a Series (one column)
```


0    110
1    130
2    105
3    125
4    100
5    120
Name: speed, dtype: int64




Code
```{python}
cars[["name", "speed"]]    # a DataFrame (note the double brackets)
```


      name  speed
0     Mini    110
1     Golf    130
2     Polo    105
3    Civic    125
4     Jazz    100
5  Corolla    120


The double brackets [[ ]] are easy to remember if you think of the inner [ ] as building a Python list of column names.
Rows. Here is the big one: pandas indexing is 0-based, whereas R is 1-based. So the first row is at position 0, not 1. Use .iloc[...] to select by integer position and .loc[...] to select by label (the row’s index).


Code
```{python}
cars.iloc[0]               # FIRST row, by position (0-based!)
```


name     Mini
brand     BMW
speed     110
doors       3
Name: 0, dtype: object




Code
```{python}
cars.loc[0, "name"]        # cell at label 0, column "name"
```


'Mini'








NoteIn a nutshell: iloc is positional, loc is by label, and counting starts at 0



df.iloc[...] is integer-position based (think “i for integer”); df.loc[...] is label based. Because our DataFrame has the default integer index, the labels happen to be 0, 1, 2, ..., so the two can look similar here — but they are different tools. And remember: the first row is position 0, not 1.

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
Filtering rows (dplyr filter)
To keep rows matching a condition, you build a boolean mask and index with it — df[df['x'] > 3]. This is the pandas version of dplyr’s filter().


Code
```{python}
cars[cars["speed"] > 115]
```


      name   brand  speed  doors
1     Golf      VW    130      5
3    Civic   Honda    125      5
5  Corolla  Toyota    120      4


There is also a tidier, more readable alternative, query(), which lets you write the condition as a string and refer to columns by bare name — much like filter() does with non-standard evaluation:


Code
```{python}
cars.query("speed > 115")
```


      name   brand  speed  doors
1     Golf      VW    130      5
3    Civic   Honda    125      5
5  Corolla  Toyota    120      4


The dplyr equivalent for reference:


Code
```{r}
# library(dplyr)
# cars |> filter(speed > 115)
subset(cars, speed > 115)   # base R version, no packages needed
```


     name  brand speed doors
2    Golf     VW   130     5
4   Civic  Honda   125     5
6 Corolla Toyota   120     4

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
Creating new columns (dplyr mutate)
Adding a column is as simple as assigning to it, df['new'] = .... This mutates the DataFrame in place.


Code
```{python}
cars["kph_to_mph"] = cars["speed"] * 0.621
cars
```


      name   brand  speed  doors  kph_to_mph
0     Mini     BMW    110      3      68.310
1     Golf      VW    130      5      80.730
2     Polo      VW    105      5      65.205
3    Civic   Honda    125      5      77.625
4     Jazz   Honda    100      5      62.100
5  Corolla  Toyota    120      4      74.520


If you prefer a non-mutating, pipe-friendly style (closer to dplyr’s mutate(), which returns a new data frame), use assign(), which returns a new DataFrame:


Code
```{python}
cars.assign(fast = cars["speed"] > 115)
```


      name   brand  speed  doors  kph_to_mph   fast
0     Mini     BMW    110      3      68.310  False
1     Golf      VW    130      5      80.730   True
2     Polo      VW    105      5      65.205  False
3    Civic   Honda    125      5      77.625   True
4     Jazz   Honda    100      5      62.100  False
5  Corolla  Toyota    120      4      74.520   True


In dplyr you would write cars |> mutate(fast = speed > 115).

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
Sorting (dplyr arrange)
Use sort_values() to order rows by one or more columns. The ascending=False argument is the analogue of wrapping a column in desc() in dplyr.


Code
```{python}
cars.sort_values("speed", ascending=False)
```


      name   brand  speed  doors  kph_to_mph
1     Golf      VW    130      5      80.730
3    Civic   Honda    125      5      77.625
5  Corolla  Toyota    120      4      74.520
0     Mini     BMW    110      3      68.310
2     Polo      VW    105      5      65.205
4     Jazz   Honda    100      5      62.100


The dplyr equivalent would be cars |> arrange(desc(speed)).

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
Grouping and summarising (dplyr group_by |> summarise)
This is the heart of data wrangling, and pandas maps onto the dplyr workflow neatly. df.groupby('group') is group_by(), and you then apply an aggregation.


Code
```{python}
cars.groupby("brand")["speed"].mean()
```


brand
BMW       110.0
Honda     112.5
Toyota    120.0
VW        117.5
Name: speed, dtype: float64


That gives the mean speed per brand — the equivalent of:


Code
```{r}
# cars |> group_by(brand) |> summarise(mean_speed = mean(speed))
aggregate(speed ~ brand, data = cars, FUN = mean)
```


   brand speed
1    BMW 110.0
2  Honda 112.5
3 Toyota 120.0
4     VW 117.5


For several summaries at once, use .agg(...), just as you would list several expressions inside summarise():


Code
```{python}
cars.groupby("brand").agg(
    mean_speed = ("speed", "mean"),
    n_cars     = ("speed", "size"),
)
```


        mean_speed  n_cars
brand                     
BMW          110.0       1
Honda        112.5       2
Toyota       120.0       1
VW           117.5       2


The ("speed", "mean") syntax names the output column mean_speed and says “take the speed column and apply mean” — closely mirroring summarise(mean_speed = mean(speed), n_cars = n()).

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
dplyr → pandas translation table
Keep this handy. Once these patterns click, most wrangling tasks are a quick mental lookup.








Task
dplyr
pandas




Filter rows
filter(speed > 115)
df[df["speed"] > 115] or df.query("speed > 115")


Select columns
select(name, speed)
df[["name", "speed"]]


Create / modify a column
mutate(fast = speed > 115)
df.assign(fast = df["speed"] > 115) or df["fast"] = ...


Arrange rows
arrange(desc(speed))
df.sort_values("speed", ascending=False)


Group and summarise
group_by(brand) |> summarise(m = mean(speed))
df.groupby("brand").agg(m=("speed", "mean"))


The pipe
df |> ... |> ...
method chaining: df.method().method()...



The last row is the key conceptual bridge: where R threads a data frame through a sequence of verbs with the pipe |>, pandas threads a DataFrame through a sequence of methods with the dot ..

title: pandas: DataFrames for Data Wrangling
text:
Going further






TipGoing further 🚀



Method chaining is the pipe. Because each pandas verb returns a DataFrame, you can chain them just like a dplyr pipeline. The reset_index() at the end turns the grouping labels back into an ordinary column (otherwise brand would live in the index):


Code
```{python}
(
    cars
    .groupby("brand")
    .agg(mean_speed=("speed", "mean"))
    .reset_index()
    .sort_values("mean_speed", ascending=False)
)
```


    brand  mean_speed
2  Toyota       120.0
3      VW       117.5
1   Honda       112.5
0     BMW       110.0


Reading top to bottom, this is cars |> group_by(brand) |> summarise(...) |> arrange(desc(mean_speed)).
Real data. Instead of building tables by hand, you would normally load them with pd.read_csv("file.csv") — the analogue of read.csv() or readr::read_csv().
Joins. pandas has df.merge(other, on="key", how="left") (and df.join(...)), which correspond to dplyr’s left_join(), inner_join() and friends.
reticulate interop. This very document mixes R and Python via reticulate, and you can pass data between them. In an R chunk, py$cars reads the Python cars DataFrame as an R data frame; in a Python chunk, r.some_r_dataframe reads an R data frame as a pandas DataFrame. For example, an R chunk could run head(py$cars) to inspect the Python object we built above, and a Python chunk could run r.cars to pull in the base-R cars data frame. This lets you wrangle in whichever language fits the task best.


You now have the core of pandas: it is the same mental model as the tidyverse, expressed with brackets and dots instead of verbs and pipes. When you get stuck, ask yourself “what would I write in dplyr?” and then translate — the table above will usually get you there.

title: How to Use AI/LLMs for your studies
text:
Large language models (LLMs) and other generative AI tools are increasingly available to students and researchers, and their use in statistical work must be governed by clear principles of academic integrity, transparency, and responsibility. When used appropriately, such tools can support learning and productivity; when misused, they risk undermining understanding, originality, and the credibility of reported results.


Generative AI tools may be used as assistive aids, rather than as substitutes for intellectual work. Appropriate uses include:

Language and Presentation Support AI tools can be used to improve the grammar and readability of text you have already written. This is acceptable, provided the underlying ideas, structure, and arguments come from you.
Clarification of Concepts AI tools are really useful for explaining mathematical concepts, especially for understanding the logic behind tricky proofs and definitions. Note that this should be used to support, not replace, lecture material and independent understanding.
Code Debugging and Syntax Assistance Generative AI can be used to help identify syntax errors and suggest alternative ways of solving problems. This is probably the best use of AI. The debugging stage of writing code used to take the longest amount of time, especially when doing it independently. But now, you can use AI tools to quickly identify issues, and more importantly, learn why they happened in the first place!

In all such cases, the AI tool functions as a supporting instrument, similar to a spell-checker, reference book, or programming forum.




Certain uses of generative AI are not appropriate in academic work:

Generating Substantive Analysis or Results It is not acceptable to use AI tools to generate analyses, interpret results, or draw conclusions that you do not fully understand or cannot independently justify.
Writing Large Sections of the Report Submitting large portions of AI-generated text as original work constitutes academic misconduct if not explicitly permitted and acknowledged. This applies even if the text is edited afterwards.
Producing Code Without Understanding Using AI to generate entire code blocks without understanding how they work is inappropriate. Statistical programming is part of the assessed intellectual work and thus constitutes academic dishonesty.
Fabrication of References, Data, or Methods AI tools may produce plausible-sounding but incorrect citations, datasets, or methodological claims. Be very careful when trusting AI outputs and be sure to fact check them!





Students are responsible for everything submitted under their name, regardless of whether AI tools were used. Here are some tips to know whether you have used AI well or not:

All results can be explained and defended orally if required.
All claims, references, and code outputs are independently verified.
If you had to do this assignment again with only the knowledge you had now, after using AI, you would not need to consult the AI for a second time.

Ultimately, generative AI tools should be viewed as assistive technologies, not as all-knowing assignment printers. Sound statistical reporting depends on human judgement and reasoning, which cannot be delegated to a probabilistic system!

title: Introduction to Report Writing
text:
“We have the duty of formulating, of summarizing, and of communicating our conclusions, in intelligible form, in recognition of the right of other free minds to utilize them in making their own decisions.” — Henri Poincaré

The subsections here will introduce core principles of statistical report writing, with a focus on clarity, structure, and effective communication. These conventions are directly relevant to the ST117 final project, ST231, and more broadly to academic and professional statistical writing.
Good report writing is not about adding complexity, but about presenting results in a way that allows the reader to understand what was done, why it was done, and what the results mean, without ambiguity or unnecessary detail.
A strong statistical report achieves three things:

it records the analysis clearly,
it makes the conclusions easy to follow,
it allows someone else to reproduce the work.


What you will learn
This section will help you decide what belongs in each report section, how much detail is enough, and how to choose the right form of presentation for your results.
This section covers:


structuring a statistical report,
reporting descriptive statistics clearly and appropriately, reporting numerical values and choosing suitable precision, presenting data using tables and graphs,
use of English in technical writing, stylistic conventions in statistics,
appropriate use of large language models and other generative AI tools.

title: Reproducibility and Workflow
text:
A report is not just its words and figures — it is the process that produced them. A good analysis is reproducible: someone else (or you, six months later) can take your files, press one button, and get exactly the same results. This page covers the habits and tools that make your work reproducible, organised, and easy to hand in or collaborate on. Across most of your degree you will write reports in RMarkdown, so everything here is framed around it.






NoteIn a nutshell: what reproducibility means



Reproducible = “rerun it, get the same answer.” If your report’s numbers and plots are produced by code that runs start-to-finish from the raw data, your work is reproducible. If they were copied by hand, tweaked in Excel, or rely on objects only in your current session, they are not — and “it worked on my machine” is the most expensive sentence in data science.



One document for code, prose and output: RMarkdown
The single most important reproducibility tool is RMarkdown (.Rmd). An RMarkdown file weaves together three things in one place:

narrative text (written in markdown),
R code chunks that run and produce results, and
the output (tables, figures, numbers) inserted automatically.

When you knit the file, RStudio runs every chunk from a clean state and assembles a polished PDF, HTML or Word document. Because the figures and numbers come directly from the code, they can never drift out of sync with your analysis — the defining feature of a reproducible report.
A minimal .Rmd begins with a YAML header that controls the output:
---
title: "My Analysis"
author: "Your Name"
date: "2026-06-26"
output: pdf_document    # or html_document, word_document
---
Code lives in chunks, whose options control what appears in the final document. A few you will use constantly:
# ```{r setup, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# library(tidyverse)
# ```

# echo    = FALSE  -> run the code but HIDE it from the report
# message = FALSE  -> suppress package start-up messages
# warning = FALSE  -> suppress warnings
# fig.align= "center", out.width = "80%"  -> tidy figures
You can also drop results straight into a sentence with inline code — a short R expression, beginning with r, written inside single backticks directly in your prose. For example, writing this line in your report:
The sample mean was {r} round(mean(myData), 1).
makes the knitted document print the actual computed mean in the sentence, so even your prose updates automatically when the data changes.






NoteIn a nutshell: knit early, knit often



The golden test of a reproducible report: restart R, then knit from scratch. If it knits cleanly, your document depends only on its code and data — not on some object you created hours ago and forgot. If it breaks, you have just found a hidden dependency before your marker does.




Organise the project, not just the file
Reproducibility starts with where your files live. Keep one self-contained folder per project, with a sensible structure:
my-project/
├── my-project.Rproj      <- an RStudio Project file
├── data/                 <- raw data (never edited by hand)
│   └── survey.csv
├── R/                    <- analysis scripts
│   └── clean-data.R
├── figures/              <- saved plots
└── report.Rmd            <- the RMarkdown report
Two rules make this portable to any machine:

Use an RStudio Project (File → New Project). It sets the working directory to the project folder automatically, so paths work for anyone who opens it.
Use relative paths, never absolute ones. Write read.csv("data/survey.csv"), not read.csv("C:/Users/you/Desktop/survey.csv") — the latter breaks the instant the file moves or someone else opens it. The here package (here::here("data", "survey.csv")) makes this bullet-proof.







ImportantNever edit your raw data by hand



Treat the raw data file as read-only. Every change — fixing a typo, removing an outlier, recoding a variable — should happen in code, so the path from raw data to result is fully recorded and repeatable. Hand-edited spreadsheets are the most common source of irreproducible analyses.




Make randomness reproducible
Anything involving random numbers — simulations, bootstrap, train/test splits, model fitting with random starts — will give different output each run unless you fix the seed. Set it once at the top so the “random” results are identical every time the report is knitted.


Code
```{r}
set.seed(123)
sample(1:100, 5)     # these five numbers are now the same on every run
```


[1] 31 79 51 14 67




Track changes with version control
Git records the full history of your project: every saved version, who changed what, and when — with the ability to roll back any mistake. Paired with GitHub, it also backs up your work to the cloud and lets you collaborate without emailing report_final_FINAL_v3.Rmd around.
RStudio has built-in Git support (tick “Create a git repository” when making a Project), so the everyday workflow is just three steps, repeated:
git add report.Rmd        # stage the files you changed
git commit -m "Add results section"   # save a snapshot, with a message
git push                  # send it to GitHub
You do not need to be a Git expert — even commit early, commit often with clear messages turns your project into a safe, navigable history instead of a single fragile file.


Record your environment
An analysis can break a year later because a package changed. Two levels of defence:

Light: end your report with sessionInfo(), which prints your R version and every package version — a permanent record of what produced the results.
Thorough: use the renv package to lock the exact package versions in a project, so anyone (including future you) can restore the identical environment and reproduce the analysis precisely.



Code
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Light: a record of versions, printed in an appendix
sessionInfo()

# Thorough: snapshot and restore an exact package environment
# install.packages("renv")
renv::init()      # start tracking this project's packages
renv::snapshot()  # save the exact versions to renv.lock
renv::restore()   # (later, elsewhere) rebuild the identical environment
```




A reproducibility checklist
Before submitting any report, run through this:

The report is an .Rmd that knits from a clean session (restart R, then knit).
All paths are relative (or via here::here()); no setwd() to a personal folder.
Raw data is untouched; all cleaning is done in code.
set.seed() is set wherever randomness is used.
Code chunks use echo=FALSE (and message/warning=FALSE) so the report shows results, not clutter — with the full code in an appendix.
The project is under version control with meaningful commits.
An environment record (sessionInfo() or renv) is included.







TipGoing further 🚀



Beyond renv, the professional reproducibility stack includes targets (a make-style pipeline that reruns only the steps whose inputs changed — invaluable for long analyses), continuous integration via GitHub Actions (which can re-knit your report automatically on every push to prove it still works), and Docker, which packages your entire computing environment — R, packages and system libraries — into a container that runs identically anywhere. These are how reproducible research scales from a coursework .Rmd to a published paper.




Summary








Habit
Tool
Why




Code + prose + output in one place
RMarkdown (.Rmd, knit)
Numbers and figures can never drift from the analysis


Self-contained project
RStudio Project + relative paths / here
Runs on any machine, not just yours


Reproducible randomness
set.seed()
Identical results every run


History and backup
Git + GitHub
Roll back mistakes; collaborate safely


Environment record
sessionInfo() / renv
Reproduces even after packages change



Reproducibility is not extra work bolted on at the end — it is a way of working that makes your reports more trustworthy, your collaboration painless, and your future self grateful. Build the habits now and every analysis you write for the rest of your degree gets easier.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
text:
A data structure is a way of organising and storing information so a computer can use it efficiently. In statistics and data science, choosing the right structure makes your code easier to write, easier to read, and often much faster.
For example, a vector is perfect for a list of numbers, while a data frame is better for a table with many variables. The right structure also helps you choose the right algorithm for the task.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
text:
A data structure is a way of organising and storing information so a computer can use it efficiently. In statistics and data science, choosing the right structure makes your code easier to write, easier to read, and often much faster.
For example, a vector is perfect for a list of numbers, while a data frame is better for a table with many variables. The right structure also helps you choose the right algorithm for the task.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
text:
Common data structures for statistics

Vectors and arrays
A vector is an ordered collection of values of the same type. In R, vectors are the simplest data structure; in Python, the closest equivalent is a numpy array.

Use a vector for a single numeric or character sequence.
Use vector operations when the same calculation applies to every element.

Example in R:


Code
```{r}
x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)
mean(x)
```


[1] 5


Example in Python:
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
x = np.array([2, 4, 6, 8])
print(x.mean())


Lists
A list can hold values of different types and structures. In R, lists are flexible containers for numbers, strings, vectors, or even other lists. In Python, dictionaries and lists serve a similar purpose.
Use a list when the items are not all the same shape or type.


Data frames and tables
A data frame is a table where each column is a variable and each row is an observation. This is the standard structure for statistical datasets.
In R, data.frame and tibble are common. In Python, pandas.DataFrame is the usual choice.
A data frame is ideal for:

storing raw data,
joining tables,
grouping and summarising by variable,
fitting models.



Dictionaries and maps
A dictionary (Python) or named list (R) stores values by key. This is useful when you need to look up values by name rather than by position.
Example in Python:
person = {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 24, 'score': 82}
print(person['score'])
Example in R:


Code
```{r}
person <- list(name = 'Alice', age = 24, score = 82)
print(person$score)
```


[1] 82

objectID: Theory of Programming/Data Structures and Algorithms.html#algorithms-in-statistics
href: Theory of Programming/Data Structures and Algorithms.html#algorithms-in-statistics
title: Data Structures and Algorithms
text:
Algorithms in statistics
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem. In statistics, algorithms manage tasks such as:

searching and filtering data,
summarising observations,
sorting and ranking values,
sampling and simulation,
fitting models.

A good algorithm is:

correct,
simple enough to understand,
efficient enough for the dataset you are using.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
text:
A simple algorithm example
Suppose you want to count how many values in a dataset are greater than 100. The algorithm is:

start a counter at zero,
look at each value in the dataset,
if the value is greater than 100, add one to the counter,
return the counter.

In R:


Code
```{r}
values <- c(70, 105, 98, 121, 115)
countOver100 <- 0
for (val in values) {
  if (val > 100) {
    countOver100 <- countOver100 + 1
  }
}
print(countOver100)
```


[1] 3


In Python:
#| eval: false
values = [70, 105, 98, 121, 115]
count_over_100 = sum(1 for val in values if val > 100)
print(count_over_100)
Both versions follow the same algorithm, but the Python example uses a more compact expression.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
section: Algorithm cost: Big O at a glance
text:
Algorithm cost: Big O at a glance
Big O notation describes how the runtime grows as the dataset gets larger. A few important ideas:

O(1): constant time. The cost does not depend on the dataset size.
O(n): linear time. The cost grows directly with the number of items.
O(n^2): quadratic time. The cost grows with the square of the number of items.


Common operations

Access one element in a vector: O(1)
Scan all rows in a table: O(n)
Nested loops over two lists: O(n^2)
Sorting a list: typically O(n log n)

In statistics, many useful operations are O(n), such as computing means, sums, and simple counts. Nested loops can be expensive for large datasets.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
Data Structures and Algorithms
section: Why this matters for modelling and machine learning
text:
Why this matters for modelling and machine learning
Data structures and algorithms are the foundation of statistical computing. When you fit a model, the software is using algorithms to:

prepare features,
compute coefficients,
search for the best parameters,
validate predictions.

Choosing the right structure makes every step faster and more reliable.
For example, a data frame is usually the best structure for a dataset, but a vector or array can be faster for numeric calculations once the dataset is prepared.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
text:
Try it yourself

Load a vector of numbers in R.
Write a function that returns the number of values greater than the mean.
Change the function to return the number of values between the 25th and 75th percentiles.

This helps you practise the two key skills in this section: choosing a structure and writing a clear algorithm.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
text:
An interpreter reads source code and executes it directly, typically one statement at a time. This makes interpreted languages easier to run interactively, which is why R and Python are popular for data analysis.
Interpreters are useful for exploration and rapid development, but they often add overhead at runtime because the code must be translated as it runs.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
text:
An interpreter reads source code and executes it directly, typically one statement at a time. This makes interpreted languages easier to run interactively, which is why R and Python are popular for data analysis.
Interpreters are useful for exploration and rapid development, but they often add overhead at runtime because the code must be translated as it runs.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
text:
What is a compiler?
A compiler translates source code into machine code or another lower-level form before the program runs. The compiled program can then execute without the overhead of line-by-line translation.
Compiled languages such as C or C++ are often faster at runtime because the instructions are already prepared for the processor.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
text:
Hybrids and bytecode
Many modern languages use a hybrid approach:

source code is compiled into bytecode,
the bytecode is executed by a virtual machine,
some systems use just-in-time (JIT) compilation to optimise code while it runs.

This gives a balance between developer productivity and runtime performance.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
text:
R and Python in practice
R and Python are usually described as interpreted languages, but the full story is more nuanced.

R parses expressions and executes them through an interpreter.
Many of R’s core functions are implemented in compiled C or C++.
Python also compiles source code to bytecode before execution.

That means a high-level command such as summing a vector can still use fast compiled code behind the scenes.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
section: Why this matters for data science
text:
Why this matters for data science
Understanding the difference between interpreters and compilers helps you know where performance comes from.

high-level code is good for writing and testing ideas quickly,
compiled code is good for tight loops and heavy numeric work,
many data science languages combine both approaches.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
text:
Key trade-offs

Interpreters: easier to use, more flexible, slower per operation.
Compilers: faster at runtime, harder to write, less interactive.

The practical choice is often to write readable high-level code first and then move the costly parts into compiled routines if needed.

title: Interpreters vs Compilers
text:
Summary
Interpreters and compilers are two ways of turning language into action. For a programming course, the important point is that high-level languages like R and Python can be both easy to write and, thanks to compiled internals, efficient enough for serious data work.

title: Purpose of Programming
text:
At its core, programming is not just about writing code or memorising syntax. Programming is the process of instructing a computer to solve a specific problem or automate a repetitive task.
Computers are incredibly fast at arithmetic, but they have zero intuition. They require explicit, logical, step-by-step instructions to do anything useful.

title: Purpose of Programming
text:
At its core, programming is not just about writing code or memorising syntax. Programming is the process of instructing a computer to solve a specific problem or automate a repetitive task.
Computers are incredibly fast at arithmetic, but they have zero intuition. They require explicit, logical, step-by-step instructions to do anything useful.

title: Purpose of Programming
text:
What is an algorithm?
An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined steps for solving a problem. In other words, it is a recipe that a computer can follow exactly.
In statistics and data science, algorithms are used for:

cleaning and preparing data,
computing summaries and statistics,
fitting models,
running simulations,
validating results.

This is why programming theory matters: it teaches you how to build the logic behind every statistical task, not just how to type code.

title: Purpose of Programming
section: Why Learn to Program in Statistics?
text:
Why Learn to Program in Statistics?
As a statistician or data scientist, programming serves three primary purposes:

Automation: Running an analysis on 5 data points by hand is easy. Running it on 5,000,000 data points requires automation.
Reproducibility: If you compute a test statistic by clicking buttons in Excel, no one can easily replicate your steps. A script records your exact logical workflow.
Simulation: When mathematical theory becomes too complex to solve analytically, we use programming to simulate data and approximate answers.

title: Purpose of Programming
text:
The Core Workflow
Every program you will ever write—whether a simple R script, a Python data pipeline, or a Java application—follows the exact same fundamental mathematical and logical loop:
\[\text{Input Data} \longrightarrow \text{Process (Your Logic)} \longrightarrow \text{Output Result}\]

Example: A Simple R Program
Here is how this operational loop looks inside an R script calculating a basic statistical mean:
# 1. INPUT: Define a vector of student exam scores
scores <- c(72, 85, 64, 91, 78)

# 2. PROCESS: Calculate the average score
avg <- sum(scores) / length(scores)

# 3. OUTPUT: Print the result to the console
print(avg)
Notice how the logic is explicitly split. The computer doesn’t “know” what an average is; we have to tell it to sum the items first, count them second, and divide third. This is how you should think about code which is that an input is taken, a finite set of instructions are executed and then the output is revealed (this is by design the definition of an algorithm).
With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), it is tempting to just ask an AI to write your scripts for you. However, relying on AI without understanding the foundation leads to major blind spots:

The Hallucination Trap: LLMs frequently invent R functions or Python libraries that do not exist, or they use outdated syntax that will break your code.
The Logic Gap: An AI can give you a block of code, but if your underlying statistical model or data structure is wrong, the output will be mathematically meaningless (“Garbage In, Garbage Out”).

The Goal of this Course: To teach you how to think like a programmer so you can write, debug, and critique code independently—whether it’s generated by you or an AI.

title: Purpose of Programming
text:
The statistical programming loop
A useful way to think about code is as a statistical workflow:

Input data,
Process it using algorithms,
Output results and diagnostics.

For example, a typical analysis may look like:

load the raw dataset,
clean and transform the variables,
fit a model or compute a statistic,
review the result and check whether it makes sense.

This loop is the same in R, Python, or any other language; the difference is only the vocabulary and syntax.
